sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There is a version of Jesus the dust is glad to let you keep. He is a good man. A wise teacher. A carpenter who said hard, true things and died too young. You can respect that Jesus the way you respect a neighbor who built a straight fence and kept his word on a handshake. You can quote him at a funeral. You can hang his picture in the hall. You can even teach your boys to admire him. What you never have to do is kneel.

That is the lie, and it is an old one. Plenty of men will tell you they believe in God and, in the same breath, tell you Jesus was only a man. The dust likes that arrangement because it leaves you in charge. A teacher can hand you rules. He cannot hand you life. So you take the rules, work them as hard as you can, and live off whatever you can wring out of the ground. Then the ground wins. It always does, because you came from it and you are headed back to it.

Psalm 119:25 is the cry of a man who has reached the end of what he can wring out: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) He does not ask for better rules. He asks for life, and he asks for it from a word that is not his own. John opens his Gospel by telling you who that Word is. Before the dust, before the ground, before the first man was shaped from it, the Word was already there — and the Word was God.

sections.heading: Written That You May Believe
pulls: A good teacher can hand you rules. Only God can hand you life. John opens his Gospel by telling you the Word was God, so you will know where to go when the rules run out.
paras: The man who wrote this book calls himself the disciple whom Jesus loved. He leaned on Jesus’ breast at the supper, and he tells you plainly that he is the one who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. He is traditionally known as John the son of Zebedee, one of the twelve. He wrote with one aim, and near the end he names it: that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

Every sign, every conversation, every night scene in this Gospel is bent toward that aim. Four volumes will walk the whole book, chapter by chapter, all the way to the empty tomb. This first one covers chapters one through five. And John does not ease you in. His opening words are the opening words of Genesis. He takes you back before the first morning and shows you who was already standing there. Read the five verses before you go on, then read them again, slower. The rest of this study leans on them the way a house leans on its footing.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD
paras: Start where John starts. In the beginning was the Word. Not that the Word came to be. Was. When the beginning began, the Word was already there. You cannot get behind Him. There is no earlier day when He was not, no shop where He was built, no quarry He was dug out of. Everything else in this book has a starting point — the fishermen, the crowds, the temple, the hill outside the city. He does not.

Why call Him the Word? Because a word is how what is inside a man comes out. You know a man by what he says. Silence keeps him hidden; speech brings him into the open. God has never been silent about Himself, and the Word is God speaking — not a sound in the air, but a Person who makes God known. John will spend twenty-one chapters letting you hear Him.

Notice what John does with Genesis. Moses wrote, In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. Then, over and over in that first chapter, God said — and it was so. Light, sky, sea, ground, seed. Everything that exists came out of the mouth of God. John reaches back to that chapter and tells you the speaking had a name. The voice that called the world out of nothing is the same One who would later sit by a well, tired from the road.

So when the dust tells you Jesus was a good teacher who came along partway through history, John puts his finger on the first line of the Bible. He was there. He was speaking. History did not produce Him. He made the world history happens in, and He will be standing there when it is over.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WITH GOD, AND GOD
paras: The Word was with God. Two things are true in this verse, and John will not let you drop either one. First, the Word is distinct. You cannot be with someone and be the same person as him. The Word faced the Father, shared His company, belonged with Him before anything was. The Son is not the Father wearing a different coat, and the Father is not the Son under another name.

Second, the Word was God. Not a lesser god. Not the first and highest creature. Verse 3 shuts that door: everything made was made through Him, so He is not one of the made things. The Word is God in the full sense — all that the Father is, with nothing missing.

Hold both and you are holding what Scripture teaches and the church confesses: one God, and within that one God the Father and the Son — and, as John will show you later, the Spirit. John does not explain how. He does not try to make it fit in your head. He tells you what is, and asks you to bow. Then he says it again so you cannot miss it: The same was in the beginning with God.

Why does this matter on a Tuesday? Because the One who went to the cross for you was not a good man trying to cover your debt with the little he had. A mere man could not carry your sin; he has his own. The Word who is God became a man and took your debt, and there is no bottom to what God can pay. When Thomas finally sees it, near the end of this book, he does not say good teacher. He says, My Lord and my God. That is where John is taking you.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ALL THINGS THROUGH HIM
pulls: The dust you came from was His material before it was ever your grave. The Word who made the ground knows what dust is, and He knows how to make something living out of it again.
paras: All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. John says it twice, once forward and once backward, the way a man checks a knot before he trusts it with a load. Every ridge, every bird, every handful of soil in your back field, the iron in the ground and the iron in your blood — made through Him. There is no corner of the world He does not own by right of having made it.

That cuts two ways. First it humbles you. The One you have treated as a tool for your plans is the One who made the hands you plan with. You are not His sponsor. You are His handiwork. Paul says the same of Christ: in him all things are held together. The ground under your boots holds because He holds it.

Then it steadies you. The world is not a machine running loose. The One who made it has not walked off the job. And the dust you came from — Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground — was His material before it was ever your grave. He knows what dust is. He made it. Which means He knows how to make something living out of it again.

Here is the wonder John is building toward. The Maker of all things did not keep His distance from what He made. The hands that shaped the first man would one day be nailed to wood by men He had shaped. The Creator walked into His own creation to rescue it. No builder ever moved into a burning house to carry out the people who set the fire. This one did.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: LIFE THAT SHINES IN THE DARK
paras: In him was life. Not in His teaching only. Not in His example. In Him. Life is not something He points to. It is something He has, the way a spring has water. Later He will say, I am the resurrection and the life. Here John tells you that was true before there was a single grave in the world.

And the life was the light of men. Life and light run together through this Gospel. The life that is in the Word is what lets a man see — see God, see himself, see where he is going. Without it, men walk in the dark and do not know where they are headed. With it, a man finally sees the truth about his sin, and in the same light sees the One who came to carry it.

Then John writes one of the most hopeful sentences in the Bible: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it. Shines — not shone once, long ago. It is still shining. And the darkness has had its full try. It had its try at the cross, when the world worked to put the light out for good. Before sunrise on the first day of the week, the tomb stood open and the light was walking in a garden.

That is your hope this week. The dark in your house, the dark in your own chest, the dark that wakes you at three in the morning — none of it has beaten the light. Not once. The light does not need your help to keep burning, and it does not need you to be strong. The Word who made you holds the life you lack, and He gives it to every man who believes in His name.

stations.verse: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
stations.question: John opens with In the beginning was the Word — before the first morning, God was already speaking Himself out; where have I treated God as silent and kept guessing at Him instead of listening to Jesus?
stations.gloss: a word; speech that carries what is in the mind
stations.live: Read John 1:1–5 aloud each morning this week before you look at your phone. Let the first voice you hear be His: ‘In the beginning was the Word.’
body: Logos is the common word for a word or a saying — not a bare sound or label, but a word that carries a thought, the inside of a man brought out. It can mean a statement or the whole of what someone teaches. In the Greek Old Testament it most often stands for the Hebrew dabar, word.

John takes that ordinary word and sets it in a class of its own: the Divine Word, a Person. John’s first letter calls Him the Word of life, and the last book of the Bible says of the One in the blood-sprinkled robe, His name is called “The Word of God.” God’s Word is not a message about Him you can take or leave. It is a Person.
The dust says God is quiet and you are left to guess at Him. Logos says God has spoken, out loud and in flesh. You do not have to guess. You have to listen.

stations.verse: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
stations.question: The Word was God, so the One who went to the cross for me was not a good man doing his best but God Himself; how does that change the way I think about whether my sin is truly paid?
stations.live: Write John 20:28 on a card and keep it in your shirt pocket. Each time your hand finds it this week, say Thomas’s words as your own: ‘My Lord and my God.’
body: Theos is the Bible’s word for God. In the Greek Old Testament it stands chiefly for Elohim, the word in In the beginning, God created, and it also renders the covenant name Yahweh. In the New Testament it usually carries the article — the God.

The word comes twice in John 1:1, and the two uses do different work. In the phrase with God, which John repeats in verse 2, theos carries the article: the Word faced a Person distinct from Himself. In the Word was God, theos stands without the article as the predicate, telling you what the Word is. Not a second god. One God, and the Word is fully that God.
The dust wants a Jesus you can admire from across the yard. Theos will not allow it. The One who bled is God, and God has not kept you at arm’s length. He came close enough to touch.

stations.verse: In him was life, and the life was the light of men.
stations.question: John says In him was life — not in His teaching or His example only, but in Him — and that life is the light men see by; what have I been trying to squeeze life out of instead of Christ Himself?
stations.gloss: a human being; man as distinct from God
stations.live: Name one place where you have been running on your own wisdom and calling it strength. Pray over it once a day this week: ‘I am a man. You are my light.’
body: Anthrōpos is the plain word for a human being, man or woman. In the Greek Old Testament it stands chiefly for adam and ish — the same adam God formed from the dust of the ground. The New Testament often uses it to set man apart from God, and sometimes to mark his frailty.

So John’s phrase has an edge. The life was in the Word; the light was for anthrōpoi — dust-made men with no light of their own. Later a crowd will reach for stones and say to Jesus, you, being a man, make yourself God. They had it backwards. He did not climb up. He came down, and the God who made men became one.
The dust says a man is enough if he works hard enough. Anthrōpos says a man is a creature who must be given light. That is no insult. It is an invitation to stop pretending you are the sun.

stations.verse: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
stations.question: John writes that the light shines in the darkness — shines, still, not once long ago; where in my house or in my own chest have I stopped expecting Christ’s light to reach today?
stations.live: Each night this week, before you turn off the lamp, name one place you saw the light of Christ that day. Then say: ‘The light shines, and the dark has not overcome it.’
body: Phainō can mean to bring something into view, but in John 1:5 it stands on its own and means to give light, to shine. It is the same sense as Peter’s lamp shining in a dark place and John’s later word that the true light already shines.

Notice the word the WEB gives you: shines. John does not say the light flickered once and went out. The light that was there in the beginning is the light still shining on the road you drive this morning. It shone at the cross, where it looked snuffed out. It shone from the open tomb. It has not stopped, and nothing in your week can make it stop.

The dust says your dark is too deep and too old, that some rooms in you are past reaching. Phainō says the light is already doing what light does. It does not wait for the darkness to give permission.

stations.verse: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
stations.question: The darkness had its full try at the light on the cross, and it hasn’t overcome it; what dark thing in me have I been treating as if it were stronger than the risen Christ?
stations.gloss: darkness; the dark of night or of the soul
stations.live: Bring one hidden thing into the light this week. Tell God by name, and if your wife or a brother in Christ needs to know, tell them: ‘This is the dark I have kept. Christ has already beaten it.’
body: Skotia means darkness. Ten of the thirteen New Testament verses where it appears belong to John’s Gospel and letters. He uses it of plain night — the dark sea, the dark morning. He also uses it of a deeper dark: a heart turned away from God that cannot see.

That second kind is the one men carry. The dark of the bottle after supper. The dark of a grudge kept warm. The dark of a secret no one at home knows. Jesus does not stand at a distance and scold it. He speaks into it: He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.

The dust says the dark gets the last word. But look where John uses skotia near the end. Mary went to the tomb while it was still dark — and saw the stone taken away. The dark was still in the sky. It had already lost the fight.

practices.title: READ THE FIRST FIVE VERSES ALOUD
practices.body: Every morning this week, read John 1:1–5 out loud before anything else gets your attention. Out loud matters, even if you mumble it over the coffee pot. You are a man who lives by words — orders, invoices, texts, the news. Let the first words of the day be the ones John wrote about the Word who was there before any day began. By Saturday you will have them close to memory, and some night soon you will need them.

practices.title: SAY WHO HE IS
practices.body: Somebody near you thinks Jesus was a good man and nothing more. Maybe a coworker, maybe your brother-in-law, maybe the man in your own mirror on a bad day. Do not argue for sport. But when it comes up, say plainly what John says: the Word was God. Then show him the verse. You do not have to win the argument. You have to be clear about who Jesus is. Clear words, said kindly, have a way of coming back to a man years later.

practices.title: THANK HIM FOR THE MADE THINGS
practices.body: John says all things were made through Him. Pick one ordinary thing each day — rain on the shop roof, bread at supper, your son’s laugh, the breath in your own chest — and thank Christ by name for making it. It will feel small. Do it anyway. A man who thanks the Maker for the made thing is learning to stop treating the world, and himself, as self-made. Gratitude is how a creature stands up straight.

practices.title: GO TO HIM FOR LIFE
practices.body: Name the thing you have been trying to squeeze life out of: the job, the paycheck, your wife’s approval, the next win, the second drink. Write it down. Beside it write, In him was life. Not in that. In Him. Pray over the paper once a day this week, and ask Christ to give you from Himself what that thing never could. Then go to work, and let the thing be what it is: a gift, not a god.

practices.title: NAME ONE DARK PLACE
practices.body: Pick the dark place you have stopped expecting to change — the silence between you and your father, the anger that leaks out at the dinner table, the habit you only feed after midnight. Name it to God in plain words. Then read verse 5 over it: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it. You are not promising to fix it by Friday. You are confessing who wins. Say it again the next morning, and the morning after that.

title: The Word Before the Dust
subtitle: from dust to the life that was in Him
keyVerse: In him was life, and the life was the light of men.

passage.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The same was in the beginning with God.
All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
In him was life, and the life was the light of men.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.

stationsIntro: Five words carry the weight of these five verses. Read each verse slowly, answer the question as the man you are and not the man you wish you were, and let the Greek open the verse a little wider.
lifeIntro: Before the first morning, the Word was with God, and all things were made through Him. He holds the life you lack and gives it as light to dust-made men. These five practices are ways to stand in that light this week.
lifePulls: The Word who was with God and was God holds the life you do not have. He does not hand you a lamp and wish you luck. He is the light, and the darkness has never beaten Him.
prayer: Father, before anything was, Your Word was with You, and Your Word was God. All things were made through Him, and so was I. I confess I have often treated Jesus as less than He is — a teacher to consult instead of God to worship. Forgive me for looking for life in the things He made instead of in Him. In Him is life. Give me that life today, and let it be light in me. Where I have kept dark places, shine into them, and do not let me hide. Thank You that the darkness has not overcome Your Son, and never will. Keep me believing, so that believing I may have life in His name. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: Before the dust, the Word was. He was with God, and He was God — not a good teacher, not a lesser god, but God Himself, distinct from the Father and one with Him. Everything that exists was made through Him, you included. The life you keep trying to squeeze out of work, money, and approval was in Him from the beginning. His light is still shining, and the dark has not beaten it. Believe Him and live.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the One who was there before the beginning. Before your grandfather broke ground on the home place, the Word was. Before the first field was cleared or the first seed went into the dirt, the Word was. Before God said let there be light, the Word was with Him, and the Word was God. You did not start this. You are not the one holding it up, and you never were.

The dust has told you that Jesus is a good man to admire and that life is something you dig for with your own two hands. But everything you have ever stood on was made through Him. The ground you work, the bones in your back, the breath you draw before dawn — none of it started with you. The One who once made a living man out of dirt is not out of His depth with yours. He can make a living man out of you. He did not lose the knack when the first Adam fell.

And He did not stay above it. The Word who made all things came down into the dark of the world He had made. Men did their worst to Him. They nailed their Maker to a beam cut from His own trees and laid Him in a tomb cut from His own rock. The darkness had its night. Then, early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary found the stone already taken away. The light had come up out of the grave before the sun did, and the dark had nothing left to throw at Him.

So carry this into the week: the darkness has not overcome Him. Not at the cross. Not at the tomb. Not in your house, and not in the hard place you quit praying about. The life that was in Him from the beginning is the life He gives to every man who believes in His name — eternal life, starting now, held by the One through whom the world was made. When the dark comes this week, and it will, you will not be facing it alone or facing it first. Lift your face off the dust. The light is still shining, and it is shining on you.
closingVerse: In him was life, and the life was the light of men.
carry: Since in him was life — in the Word who was with God and was God, not in your rules or your effort — where will you go looking for life this week?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men carry a picture of God they never chose. It was drawn early — by a hard father, a preacher who shouted, a church where nobody smiled, a boss who never once said well done. In that picture God stands at the far end of a long hallway with His arms folded, keeping a file. You can get closer if you clean up enough. You can be counted His if you were born into the right family and kept the right rules. But you never quite know where you stand, because you have never seen His face. All you have is the distance, and the sound of your own boots on the floor.

The dust works with that picture. It tells you God is far off and hard to read. It tells you that belonging to Him is something you inherit or earn — your grandmother’s faith, your years in the pew, your record at home and at work. And when the record goes bad, it tells you the door has shut. So you either work harder or you quit walking toward Him at all. Some men do both in the same week — grind on Monday, give up by Thursday, and start the whole thing over on Sunday.

Set beside that picture the old prayer that names exactly where the soul is lying: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The man who prays it does not ask God to stay far off and grade him. He asks to be raised by a word. John 1:6–18 tells you that Word came the whole distance, took on flesh, and showed you the Father’s face — and the face is full of grace and truth.

sections.heading: A Witness, a Refusal, and a Birth
pulls: You were never meant to guess at God from a long way off. The Word became flesh and closed the distance, so that you could look at Jesus and see the Father’s face.
paras: These verses finish John’s opening. Verses 1–5 told you who the Word is before time. Verses 6–18 bring Him into the world. First comes a man named John — not the writer of this book, but the one God sent ahead of Jesus to testify. Then the hard news: the Word came to the world He made and to His own people, and they did not receive Him. John does not soften that. He wants you to feel the weight of it before he gives you what comes next.

Then the good news that runs underneath the rest. Some did receive Him, and to them He gave the right to become God’s children — a birth from God, not from blood or effort. And the Word who did the giving became flesh, and lived among us. Read the thirteen verses through before you go on. Watch the light of verse 5 walk into the room and sit down. Then read verse 14 once more by itself, out loud, slowly, because the whole Gospel hangs on it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A MAN SENT TO TESTIFY
paras: There came a man, sent from God, whose name was John. Notice what kind of man he is. He is not the light. The writer says so flatly: He was not the light, but was sent that he might testify about the light. His whole job was to point. A witness does not make the facts. He tells what he has seen, and then he steps out of the way.

That is a relief to a man who has been trying to be his own light, or everybody else’s. You were never meant to be the source. Your father was not, your pastor is not, and you are not. The most any man can be is a finger pointing past himself to Christ. John was content with that. He did not need the crowd to remember his name, only the name of the One he pointed to.

And look at why he came: that all might believe through him. Believing is the point of the testimony — the same aim the whole Gospel names at its close. God sends witnesses because He wants men to believe and live. He is not hiding from you. He is sending word ahead, the way a man sends his son down the road to tell the neighbors he is coming.

Then John names the light he pointed to: The true light that enlightens everyone was coming into the world. True — the real thing, not a copy or a reflection. Every other light a man follows is borrowed or false. This one was on the road, walking toward the world He made. You do not have to light Him or carry Him. You have to look where the witness is pointing.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE WORLD DID NOT KNOW HIM
paras: He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him. Read that slowly and let it sting. The Maker walked across His own ground, and the ground did not know Him. Men who ate bread from His fields did not know the One who sent the rain on them. They bargained in His markets, fished His lake, and buried their dead in His hills, and they looked right past Him.

Then it comes closer: He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him. Israel had the promises, the law, the temple, the prophets. And when He stood in front of them, most turned away. Later in this Gospel they will tell Him, Our father is Abraham, as though being born into the right family settled everything. They did not think they needed Him, and the ones who think that are the hardest to reach.

Do not read that with your arms crossed. Pride does the same work in a churchgoing man. The men who know the most about God are often the slowest to bow to Him. You can sit in a pew for forty years, know every hymn, give every month, and still keep Christ standing on the porch — welcome as a guest, never let in as Lord of the house.

This is the darkness of verse 5 with a face on it. It is not ignorance only. It is refusal. And it is the condition every man is born in. Left to yourself, you would have done what they did. That is why what comes next has to be the work of God, or it will not happen at all.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: BORN OF GOD
pulls: Not of blood, not of effort, not of any man’s will. If you believe in His name, you were born of God, and no family record or bad year can unwrite a birth.
paras: But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name. There is the turn. Not everyone refused. Some received Him, and John tells you what receiving Him means: believing in His name. To them He gave the right. Gave. You do not earn a right like that. You are handed it, the way a father hands his grown son a key to the house.

Then John tells you where these children come from: who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. Three doors shut. Not of blood — you cannot inherit this from your mother’s faith or your family name. Not of the will of the flesh — you cannot want it hard enough to make it happen. Not of the will of man — no preacher, no aisle, no card signed at the back of a tent can produce it.

But of God. The new birth is His work, start to finish. A baby does not birth himself. A dead man does not raise himself. You came into this world alive in body and dead toward God, and only God could give you the life you lacked. When He gives it, the man He has made alive believes. Faith is not the price of the birth. It is the first breath of it. Watch the order John keeps: God gives the right, God gives the birth, and the man who is born of Him receives and believes.

So if you have believed in His name, stop asking whether your pedigree is good enough. You have a better one. You were born of God, and what God has begotten He does not disown. Your family name did not get you in, and your worst year cannot put you out.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: FULL OF GRACE AND TRUTH
paras: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. The One who was God, through whom all things were made, became a man — real skin, real hunger, real tiredness at the end of a long walk. He did not stop being God. He took on what He was not and kept what He was. He lived His life right among the men who would refuse Him, close enough to be touched and close enough to be spit on.

We saw his glory, John says. He was there. And the glory was not what men expected. It was full of grace and truth. Christ could have come as the avenger of a broken law. He came instead with both hands full. He did not give men what they had earned. He kept the law in their place and then carried its curse.

Then John piles it up: From his fullness we all received grace upon grace. Grace laid on grace, each new gift landing before the last one is used up. For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ. The law told the truth about you and left you there. Christ brought the truth and the grace together.

And last, the answer to the oldest question a man can ask: what is God like? No one has seen God at any time. Moses asked, Please show me your glory, and was told, my face shall not be seen. He got a passing glimpse from a cleft in the rock. But the one and only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him. Look at Jesus touching the leper. Look at Him feeding the hungry and forgiving the guilty. That is the Father’s face.

stations.verse: The same came as a witness, that he might testify about the light, that all might believe through him.
stations.question: John came as a witness, sent so that all might believe through him, and he was not the light himself; who in my house or at my work needs me to point them past me to Christ this week?
stations.live: Write down the name of the person whose witness first pointed you to Christ. Thank God for that person by name, and if they are still living, call or write and tell them so this week.
body: Martyria is witness, testimony, evidence — what a man says on the stand about what he knows. Mark uses it of the trial of Jesus, where their testimony didn’t agree with each other. But the word is most at home with John: twenty-six of its thirty-three New Testament verses fall in John’s Gospel and letters and in Revelation, most often of witness to Christ.

John the Baptist came as a witness. So did the writer of this book, and the last chapter signs off: We know that his witness is true. The whole Gospel is sworn testimony. You are not reading a man’s theory about Jesus. You are reading what eyewitnesses saw and would not stop saying.

The dust says faith is a guess in the dark. Martyria says it rests on testimony, and the weightiest testimony of all is God’s own, given about His Son: God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.

stations.verse: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
stations.question: The Word became flesh, and lived among us, and the glory men saw in Him was that of the one and only Son of the Father; where have I kept God at a distance He Himself closed by coming in flesh?
stations.gloss: one and only; the only child of a parent
stations.live: When you doubt God’s heart toward you this week, do not try to reason it out. Go to the cost and say it aloud: ‘The Father gave His only Son for me. He will not hold back from me now.’
body: Monogenēs means only — the only son or only daughter of a parent. Luke uses it of the widow’s son carried out dead at Nain and of the father who begged Jesus, he is my only child. The Greek Old Testament uses it of Jephthah’s daughter: She was his only child.

Every use carries the weight of a parent with one child and no spare. Hebrews uses it of Isaac, Abraham’s one and only son. When John uses it, he uses it only of Christ — here, in 1:18, in 3:16 and 3:18, and in his first letter. The Son is not one of many. He is the Father’s only, and the Father gave Him.
The dust says God gave you what He could spare. Monogenēs says He gave the only One He had: God has sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him.

stations.verse: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
stations.question: Christ came full of grace and truth, telling the whole truth about my sin and holding out grace for all of it; what truth about myself have I been afraid to face because I doubt the grace that comes with it?
stations.live: Name the sin you think has drained God’s patience with you. Bring it to Him again and say: ‘You are full of grace and truth. Your grace is not running low for me.’
body: Plērēs means full, filled. It is used of what was gathered after the crowd ate — twelve baskets full — and of grain that has come all the way in, the full grain in the ear. It is used of a man’s inner life too: Jesus returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit.

Luke uses the same word for a man at the other end: a man full of leprosy. That is the meeting John describes. A man full of sickness falls on his face before the Man full of grace and truth, and the fuller one wins. Jesus touched him, and the leprosy left him.

The dust says grace runs out — that you have used up your share and are living on what is left. Christ is not a well that goes dry in August. From his fullness we all received grace upon grace, and the fullness is no smaller for all the giving.

stations.verse: No one has seen God at any time. The one and only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him.
stations.question: No one has seen God at any time, but the Son who is in the bosom of the Father knows Him from the closest place there is; whose report about God am I trusting over His?
stations.gloss: bosom; the place of closest nearness
stations.live: Pray once this week without asking for anything. Sit with Christ the way John sat at the supper, and say: ‘Lord, I am near You because You brought me near.’
body: Kolpos is the bosom, the chest, and from there the place of closest nearness. Luke uses it of the beggar carried by angels to Abraham’s bosom. It can also mean the fold of a robe gathered at the belt and used as a pocket. The word turns up in only six New Testament verses, and John has two of them.

John says the Son is in the bosom of the Father — not was, is. He came down and lived among men, and He never left that nearness. Then, at the supper, John uses the same word of a disciple leaning against Jesus’ breast. The Son at the Father’s side. The disciple at the Son’s.

The dust says God keeps men at arm’s length. Kolpos draws the line of nearness the other way. In Christ you are not left standing outside the door. You are brought in close enough to lean, and the One you lean on is the One the Father holds.

stations.verse: No one has seen God at any time. The one and only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him.
stations.question: The unseen Father has been declared by His Son; when I watch Jesus touch the leper and forgive the guilty in these Gospels, what does that tell me about how the Father looks at me?
stations.gloss: to lead out; to unfold, tell in full
stations.live: Read one story from the Gospels each day this week. When you finish each one, say aloud: ‘So this is what my Father is like.’
body: Exēgeomai means to lead or show the way, and from there to unfold, to tell in full. The two disciples back from Emmaus related the things that happened along the way. Paul, back in Jerusalem, reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles. It is the word for telling a thing all the way through.

So when John says the Son has declared him, he means Jesus laid the Father out in full. Every touch, every word, every meal with sinners is the Father being unfolded in front of your eyes. Jesus will say it Himself: He who has seen me has seen the Father.

The dust paints God from your worst memories. Exēgeomai hands the brush back to the Son. If you want to know what God is like, do not look at the man who failed you. Look at Jesus, and keep looking until the old picture fades.

practices.title: POINT PAST YOURSELF
practices.body: John the Baptist was sent to testify about the light, and he knew he was not it. This week, find one conversation where you can point to Christ without making yourself the subject. Not the story of how hard you have worked at it — His story. Tell a friend, a son, or a man at work one thing Jesus has done. Then stop talking and let Christ be the one he remembers. You are a pointer, not the point.

practices.title: RETIRE YOUR PEDIGREE
practices.body: Write down what you have leaned on to feel right with God: the church you grew up in, your mother’s prayers, your years of giving, your clean record next to the other men on the crew. Then read verse 13 over the list. Not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. Thank Him that your place in His family rests on His work, and tear up the paper. Throw it in the burn barrel if you have one.

practices.title: RECEIVE INSTEAD OF EARNING
practices.body: John says the right to be God’s children is given to those who receive Him. Receiving is not working. A man with full hands cannot take a gift until he sets something down. This week, when you catch yourself trying to make up for a bad day with a better one, stop and receive instead. Pray: Lord, I believe in Your name, and I take what You give. Then go do your work as a son, not as a hired man hoping to be kept on through the winter.

practices.title: COUNT THE GRACE UPON GRACE
practices.body: Each evening before you sleep, name three graces from the day — a hot meal, a patient word from your wife, a sin you were kept from, a debt you were forgiven. Say them out loud, even if only the dog is listening. John says you have received grace upon grace from His fullness. Counting it will not add to it. But it will open your eyes to how much has been falling on you all along, even on the days you called empty.

practices.title: LOOK AT JESUS TO SEE THE FATHER
practices.body: Take the picture of God you have carried since you were a boy — the folded arms, the file He keeps on you — and set it beside Jesus in the Gospels. Read Luke 5:12–13, the leper. Read it twice. Then ask, Is this what God is like? John says yes. The Son has declared Him. Let Jesus redraw the picture, one story at a time. The old picture took years to draw. Give the new one more than a week.

title: Full of Grace and Truth
subtitle: from dust to the glory we have seen
keyVerse: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

passage.text: There came a man, sent from God, whose name was John.
The same came as a witness, that he might testify about the light, that all might believe through him.
He was not the light, but was sent that he might testify about the light.
The true light that enlightens everyone was coming into the world.
He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world didn’t recognize him.
He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him.
But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:
who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
John testified about him. He cried out, saying, “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me, for he was before me.’ ”
From his fullness we all received grace upon grace.
For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ.
No one has seen God at any time. The one and only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him.

stationsIntro: These five words carry John from the witness at the river to the Son at the Father’s side. Take each verse slowly, answer it as yourself, and let the Greek show you more of the face God has turned toward you.
lifeIntro: The Word who was God became flesh, lived among men, and showed you the Father’s face. He gives the right to be God’s children to every man who believes in His name. Here are five ways to live inside that gift this week.
lifePulls: The law told you the truth about yourself and left you there. Christ brought the truth and the grace together, and from His fullness you receive grace upon grace — not a ration, a flood.
prayer: Father, no one has seen You at any time, but Your Son has made You known. Thank You that the Word became flesh and lived among us. I confess I have pictured You far off, waiting for me to measure up. I have leaned on my family, my habits, and my record instead of on Christ. Thank You that I was born of You, not of blood or effort or any man’s will. Let me see Your Son’s glory, full of grace and truth. From His fullness give me grace upon grace today. Make me a witness who points past himself to the light. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, no one has seen You at any time, but Your Son has made You known.
Thank You that the Word became flesh and lived among us.
I confess I have pictured You far off, waiting for me to measure up.
I have leaned on my family, my habits, and my record instead of on Christ.
Thank You that I was born of You, not of blood or effort or any man’s will.
Let me see Your Son’s glory, full of grace and truth.
From His fullness give me grace upon grace today.
Make me a witness who points past himself to the light.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: The Word became flesh. God did not stay far off grading you. He came the whole distance, lived among men, and showed you His face in Jesus — full of grace and truth. Your place in His family does not come from blood, effort, or anybody’s will but His. If you believe in His name, you were born of God. From Christ’s fullness you receive grace upon grace. Look at Him, and you have seen the Father.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, because God has turned His face toward you. His are the hands that worked a carpenter’s bench. His are the feet that walked the roads of Galilee and got as dirty as yours. His are the eyes that met a man full of leprosy and did not look away. This is the glory John saw — not far off in a cloud, but close enough to touch, full of grace and truth. God has not hidden His face from you. He has shown it to you in His Son.

The dust has kept you at the end of a long hallway, guessing at God from what your father was or what your failures say. You thought you had to be born right or work hard to be counted His. But the Word did not wait for you to make the walk. He came the whole way to you. He became flesh, and lived among us — your kind of flesh, the kind that gets tired and hungry and cold, the kind that can be buried. He did not keep His distance from your dust. He took it on, and He has never set it down.

And He came to make sons. To every man who receives Him, who believes in His name, He gives the right to become God’s children. Not by blood. Not by effort. Not by any man’s will. By God. That right was paid for at the cross, where the one and only Son gave Himself up for men who had refused Him. It was sealed when He walked out of the grave alive in the same flesh He took, with the wounds still in His hands.

Here is what you carry into Monday. The Son who is in the bosom of the Father has brought you near. You do not have to guess at God’s heart anymore. You have seen it in Jesus. And from His fullness you will keep receiving grace upon grace, the way dry pasture keeps taking rain — tomorrow’s grace laid on top of today’s, more than your worst week can use up. Stand up out of the dust. You are not a stranger at the door. You are a son with a place at the table, and the Son of the Father set it for you.
closingVerse: The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.
carry: The Word became flesh, and lived among us — God came the whole distance to you, full of grace and truth; what part of your life will you stop holding at arm’s length from Him this week?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man keeps a ledger he never shows anyone — not the one at the bank, the other one. The words you said to your boy in the driveway are in it. So is the money that went where it should not have gone, and the second drink that turned into the fourth. So is the silence you have kept toward your wife for three weeks because breaking it would cost you something. You know the entries by heart, and you add to them more often than you cross them off.

The dust tells you that ledger is yours to settle. It says the only way out is to carry it — to work the balance down a little at a time, to make up for it with overtime of the soul. Be kinder next week. Give more. Keep your head down until the numbers look better. The dust is patient. It will let you carry it as long as you like, so long as you never set it down. Some men carry it for forty years and call it humility. It is not humility. It is a load you were never built to lift, and it is grinding you into the ground.

You know that ground by feel. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The man who says that has not run short on effort. He has run out of strength. The word that revives him in John 1 is no better plan for paying down the debt. A man is walking toward the Jordan, and another man is pointing at Him and crying out, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.

sections.heading: A Witness Who Kept Pointing Away
pulls: The dust says your sin is yours to carry until you have worked it off. John points at a man walking up the riverbank and says the carrying has been laid on Someone else.
paras: The Gospel has already introduced this man: There came a man, sent from God, whose name was John. He is not the John who wrote the book. He is the one Matthew calls John the Baptizer, a man drawing crowds to the river with a hard word and river water. The writer gives him one job in these chapters. He is a witness. The questions on the first day are all about John; the answers he gives are all about Jesus. This is John’s testimony, the passage opens, and every sentence he speaks in it points away from himself.

The scene runs over two days at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing. On the first day a delegation of priests and Levites comes down from Jerusalem with questions. On the second, Jesus Himself comes walking toward the water. Read all sixteen verses before you go further, and watch where John’s finger goes. It never once points at John.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: I AM NOT THE CHRIST
paras: The men from Jerusalem come with one question: Who are you? It is a fair thing to ask. John has the crowds. He has the river and the hard preaching and the people going down into the water. A man with that kind of following could have been anything he wanted to be that afternoon.

Look at how the writer sets down his answer. He declared, and didn’t deny, but he declared, “I am not the Christ.” Three verbs for one short sentence. The writer wants you to see that John did not dodge. He did not let them think something flattering for a day or two and correct it later. He put it on the table plainly. I am not the one you are waiting for. They try again: Are you Elijah? He says, I am not. Are you the prophet? One word: No. Each answer is shorter than the last.

That is a rare kind of strength, and most men carry very little of it. You know how good it feels to be taken for more than you are. The foreman who lets the crew think the fix was his idea. The man who lets his church believe his house is in better order than it is. John will not do it. The Christ is standing somewhere in that crowd, and John will not take one inch of the room that belongs to Him.

Here is the grace under it. A man is free to say I am not only when he knows Who is. John is not anxious about his own size. He knows the Christ has come, and he knows he is not Him. He has been sent ahead of the One who comes after him, and that is enough to make him small and glad.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A VOICE AND A SANDAL STRAP
paras: Pressed for something they can take home, John reaches for Isaiah. I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said. Not a name. A voice. A voice is the most passing thing a man owns. It carries over the water, rolls off the far bank, and is gone. Nobody builds a monument to a voice. John is content to be breath spent on getting a road ready for Someone else.

The men from the Pharisees press harder. If he is not the Christ, why then do you baptize? John does not defend his credentials. He points again. I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you don’t know. The One they came looking for is already in the crowd, close enough to touch, and they cannot see Him. They have studied the promises for years, and they walk right past the Man the promises are about.

Then John measures himself against that One and comes up short on purpose: whose sandal strap I’m not worthy to loosen. He picks the smallest service he can think of — a strap at another man’s feet — and says he is not fit even for that. He is not putting on a show of humility. He is telling the truth about the distance between a sinner and the Son of God.

Do not miss what that does for you. If the greatest preacher on that riverbank could not stoop low enough to touch Christ’s sandal, you were never going to reach Him by climbing. He will have to come to you. The distance you could not close, He closes. And the very next day, He comes walking.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: BEHOLD, THE LAMB OF GOD
pulls: A lamb on an altar covered sin for a season, and then the altar needed another lamb. The Lamb of God does not cover your sin for a season. He takes it away, and He never has to be offered twice.
paras: The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him. John does not wait for Jesus to speak. He points, and he says the sentence this whole week hangs on: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.

In the Scriptures of Israel, a lamb meant death in another’s place. Abraham, climbing the mountain with his son and the wood, said God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering. On the night of the Passover the Lord said of the lamb’s blood on the door, When I see the blood, I will pass over you. Isaiah saw a servant who went as a lamb that is led to the slaughter. Year after year the altars ran red, and the sin kept coming back, because it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins.

Now John points at a man and says: there. That one. Not a lamb Israel brought to God, but the Lamb of God — the one God Himself provides. He does not cover sin for a season. He takes it away. And not one nation’s sin only, but the sin of the world: every kind of man, from every place, with every kind of debt.

Then John adds, he was before me. John came first. Jesus was before him anyway, because the Lamb walking up the riverbank is the Word who was with God in the beginning. Only One who is God could carry what John says this One carries. John himself says I didn’t know him — his whole ministry of water existed for one reason: that he would be revealed to Israel. The sin you have been carrying has somewhere to go. It goes on Him.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE SPIRIT REMAINED ON HIM
paras: John gives one more piece of testimony. I have seen the Spirit descending like a dove out of heaven, and it remained on him. He did not guess who the Lamb was. God had told him what to watch for: On whomever you will see the Spirit descending and remaining on him is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.

Mark the word remained. The Spirit did not light on Jesus and lift off again, the way a bird lights on a fence post. He stayed. Isaiah had said of the coming King, Yahweh’s Spirit will rest on him, and here is the Man on whom God’s Spirit rests without leaving. At that river the Father who sent John, the Son who came up from the water, and the Spirit who came down are all at work — one God, three Persons, all of it bent toward your rescue.

And this One does more than carry the Spirit. He gives Him. John baptized in water. Water washes the outside of a man and runs off into the dirt. Jesus baptizes in the Holy Spirit — He puts the life of God inside a man who had none. The Lamb takes the sin away. The Spirit He pours out makes a new man where the old one lay.

John ends where every true witness ends. I have seen, and have testified that this is the Son of God. He has nothing to add. That one sentence is the reason he was born, and it is the reason this Gospel was written: that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

stations.verse: He declared, and didn’t deny, but he declared, “I am not the Christ.
stations.question: With crowds at the river, John declared, and didn’t deny, that he was not the Christ; where have I let the people around me lean on me as if I could do for them what only Christ can?
stations.gloss: to agree with; to acknowledge openly; to confess
stations.live: Name one sin to God this week in plain words, the way you would name a broken part at the parts counter. No excuses attached. Then say what He says: ‘He is faithful and righteous to forgive.’
body: Homologeō comes from a word meaning of one mind. Its senses run from speaking the same language, to agreeing, to acknowledging or confessing openly. Twenty-three New Testament verses use it, and in John 1:20 it stands with no object. John simply confessed.

To confess is to agree with God — to say about a thing what He says. John says about himself what is true: I am not the Christ. The same verb carries If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins — agreeing with God about your sin — and if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord — agreeing with God about His Son.

The dust wants you to keep the kinder version of yourself in front of God. But He already knows the worst and has said what He will do with it. Agree with Him. Confession is not the price of forgiveness. It is a man saying yes to what Christ has already settled.

stations.verse: He said, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.
stations.question: Asked who he was, John called himself the voice of one crying in the wilderness, sent to make way for Another; how much of what I say about my faith makes a name for me instead of making way for Christ?
stations.gloss: to cry out; to call aloud
stations.live: Once this week, pray out loud where no one hears you but God — in the truck, out by the back field. Not a speech. A cry: ‘Jesus, have mercy on me.’
body: Boaō means to cry or call out. It carries feeling — joy, fear, and the like — unlike the words for a harsh or wordless shout. Twelve New Testament verses use it, and once it means calling on God for help, of His chosen ones who are crying out to him day and night.

John’s cry is a voice raised over open country to clear a road for the King. The blind man near Jericho used the same verb when he cried, have mercy on me. And on the cross the Son Himself took it up: Jesus cried with a loud voice, forsaken in the place of men like you.

The dust wants you quiet — your need kept close, your sin unspoken, your mouth shut about Jesus. But the Father hears His chosen ones day and night, and the Son cried out once in the dark so that no cry of yours for mercy would go unheard.

stations.verse: He is the one who comes after me, who is preferred before me, whose sandal strap I’m not worthy to loosen.
stations.question: The greatest preacher on that riverbank said he was not worthy to loosen Christ’s sandal strap; where am I still trying to climb near enough to God on my own record, instead of letting Christ come to me?
stations.gloss: a sandal; a sole bound under the foot
stations.live: Take one job this week that nobody wants — the dishes, the dump run, the cleanup after everyone leaves — and do it for someone who will not notice. Do it as a son already welcomed home, not to earn the welcome.
body: Hypodēma is a sole bound under the foot — a sandal, plainly. It appears in ten verses of the New Testament, among them the command at the burning bush: Take off your sandals, for the place where you stand is holy ground.

John picks a strap at another man’s feet and says he is not worthy to touch it. That is the right distance between a sinner and the Holy One. But watch where the word turns up in Luke. When the lost son comes home, his father calls out, Put a ring on his hand, and sandals on his feet.

The dust says you must earn your way back into the house, one low job at a time. The Father does not wait for that. He sees the son a long way off, runs, and puts sandals on feet that had no right to them. The man unfit to loosen Christ’s sandal is the man Christ’s Father dresses for home.

stations.verse: The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
stations.question: John had crowds of his own, yet he pointed them all to Jesus as the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world; what besides the Lamb have I been counting on to deal with my sin?
stations.gloss: to lift up; to carry; to take away
stations.live: Each time you set down something heavy this week — a feed sack, a toolbox, an armload of firewood — let your hands remind you of 1:29, and say: ‘The Lamb of God took my sin away.’
body: Airō has three senses: to raise or lift up, to bear or carry, and to take away or remove. It is found in ninety-seven verses of the New Testament. It is used of Christ taking away sin here and in John’s first letter: he was revealed to take away our sins, and no sin is in him.

All three senses meet at the cross. He lifts the load, He carries it, and He takes it off the premises. John uses the same verb later, when the crowd shouts Away with him. They meant to be rid of Jesus. In that same hour God was ridding the world of its sin — on Him.

The dust tells you sin is a sack you haul until you die. Airō says it has been picked up by Someone else and carried off. You are not asked to haul it farther. You are asked to believe He took it, and to stop picking it back up.

stations.verse: John testified, saying, “I have seen the Spirit descending like a dove out of heaven, and it remained on him.
stations.question: John saw the Spirit come down and remain on Jesus, the sign that He is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit; what in me have I tried to scrub clean on the outside that only His Spirit can make new?
stations.live: Each morning this week, before the first cup of coffee, read 1:32 and say it once: ‘The Spirit rests on Him, and I am in Him.’ Let that be the first word of your day, before the news or the weather.
body: Peristera is simply a dove, and in the Greek Old Testament it chiefly renders the Hebrew word for dove. Ten New Testament verses carry it, and three of them are in John: here at the river, and twice in the next chapter, in the temple where those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves had set up.

The word sits at the start of Jesus’ life and at the start of His ministry. As a baby He was brought to the temple with the offering the law named: A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. At the Jordan the Spirit came like a dove and stayed. The Son who came low from His first day is the Son on whom the Spirit settles.

The dust says heaven hovers over you, undecided. The Spirit did not hover over Jesus. He came down and remained. Every man joined to Christ by faith stands under that same settled favor, because he stands in Him.

practices.title: SAY WHAT YOU ARE NOT
practices.body: John answered three questions about himself with three denials. Find the place where you let people think more of you than is true — the competence at work, the calm at church, the faith you describe better than you live it. Correct it once this week, plainly and without a speech. Let the man who admires you see the real size of you. You can afford to be small. Christ is already standing among you. He has no need of your reputation, and you no longer need to guard it.

practices.title: LAY THE LOAD ON THE LAMB
practices.body: Name the sin you have been carrying longest, the one you keep working off and never finish. Write it down. Read John 1:29 over it slowly. Then pray, out loud if you can: ‘Lamb of God, You took this away. I will stop hauling it.’ Do this on the morning it feels heaviest, before work, before the dust has its say. The paper is not the point. The point is where the weight goes, and it goes on Him.

practices.title: TAKE THE LOW JOB
practices.body: John said he was unfit to loosen a sandal strap. Pick one task this week that sits below your title and do it without being asked — the clogged gutter, the floor nobody sweeps, the long drive to pick up someone else’s kid. Do it as a man who has been served by the Son of God, who came all the way down for you. You are not earning anything. You are answering grace, and the low place is where you will find Him.

practices.title: POINT AWAY FROM YOURSELF
practices.body: John’s voice cleared a road for Another. In one conversation this week — with your son, a man on the crew, a neighbor at the feed store — say one true sentence about Jesus and then stop talking. Not a sermon. A finger pointed at the Lamb: ‘He takes away sin. He took away mine.’ Leave the rest to the Spirit He gives. John did not convert anyone at the river. He pointed, and the Lamb did the rest.

practices.title: REST UNDER THE SPIRIT WHO REMAINED
practices.body: The Spirit came down on Jesus and stayed. When you wake before dawn sure that God is reconsidering you, get up and read John 1:32–34 aloud at the table. You stand in the Son the Father sent, the Son the Spirit rests on. His standing with the Father is not up for review this week, and because you are in Him, neither is yours. Go back to bed a man under settled favor.

title: Behold, the Lamb of God
subtitle: from dust to the sin taken away
keyVerse: The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!

passage.text: This is John’s testimony, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”
He declared, and didn’t deny, but he declared, “I am not the Christ.”
They asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the prophet?” He answered, “No.”
They said therefore to him, “Who are you? Give us an answer to take back to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”
He said, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.”
The ones who had been sent were from the Pharisees.
They asked him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?”
John answered them, “I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you don’t know.
He is the one who comes after me, who is preferred before me, whose sandal strap I’m not worthy to loosen.”
These things were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
This is he of whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who is preferred before me, for he was before me.’
I didn’t know him, but for this reason I came baptizing in water: that he would be revealed to Israel.”
John testified, saying, “I have seen the Spirit descending like a dove out of heaven, and it remained on him.
I didn’t recognize him, but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me, ‘On whomever you will see the Spirit descending and remaining on him is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’
I have seen, and have testified that this is the Son of God.”

stationsIntro: Read each verse aloud before you answer the question under it. Every word in this passage points past the witness to the Lamb — let it point you the same way.
lifeIntro: God has provided the Lamb. The sin of the world was laid on Him, and the Spirit rests on Him without leaving. What follows is what a man does with his hands and his mouth when he believes that. None of it adds to what the Lamb finished. All of it flows from it.
lifePulls: John spent his whole voice pointing at someone else. That is the freedom of a forgiven man: he no longer needs to be the center of the room, because the Lamb has already carried what he was hiding.
prayer: Father, You provided the Lamb when I had nothing to bring. Your Son walked toward the river, and He walked toward the cross, for me. I agree with You about my sin. I name it, and I lay it on Him. He took it away. Keep me from carrying what He already carried. Make me small enough to point away from myself. Let my voice clear a road for Jesus at home and at work this week. When old sins come back to mind, turn my eyes to the Lamb. Your Spirit rests on Him and does not leave; keep me in Him. In Jesus’ name, amen.

I agree with You about my sin. I name it, and I lay it on Him.

Make me small enough to point away from myself.
Let my voice clear a road for Jesus at home and at work this week.

bottomLine: John had the crowd and the river, and he spent both pointing away from himself. He was not the Christ, not worthy of a sandal strap, only a voice. Then he saw Jesus and named Him: the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. The dust says you carry your own sin until it is paid off. Behold the Lamb. Lay it on Him and leave it there.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and look where John is pointing. Look past the riverbank and the crowd. Look past the men from Jerusalem with their questions. Look past the preacher standing in the water, who would not take one inch of the glory for himself. Look at the Man walking down to the Jordan — the One who was before John, the Word who was with God, coming toward you in plain daylight.

You have carried your ledger a long way. You have worked it down in good weeks and watched it climb in bad ones. You have called the carrying faithfulness. But that load was never yours to haul to the end. God provided the Lamb, as He told Abraham on the mountain He would, and the Lamb did not merely cover your sin for one more year. He lifted it. He bore it. He took it away. Every Passover lamb, every bull and goat, every altar fire in Israel was a finger pointing down the years at this one Man.

That is why the cross holds no half-measures. When the crowd cried Away with him, they meant to be rid of Jesus. God meant to be rid of your sin. Both happened on the same afternoon, on the same Man, as He went out bearing His cross. And on the first day of the week the same plain verb turned up again, at a garden tomb: the stone had been taken away. The Lamb who bore your sin was not held by the grave. He is the One revealed to take away our sins, and no sin is in him, and He will never be offered again, because He never needs to be.

So set it down this Tuesday. Lay it on the Lamb and leave it there. The Spirit came down on Him and remained, and you are joined to Him by faith; the Father’s favor rests where you now stand. Go to work as a man whose sin has been taken away — not trimmed, not put off, taken away — and let your voice, like John’s, point to Him. When the old entries come back to mind on the drive home, answer them with this week’s verse. Behold the Lamb. He took it away.
closingVerse: The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
carry: When John pointed to the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, he meant your sin too; what entry in your ledger will you stop carrying this week and leave on Him?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men picture heaven as a locked building. They have seen lights on inside. They have heard that God lives there. But the door is shut, and the only way in anyone ever showed them is a ladder they have to build and climb themselves — a rung for every good year, a rung for every Sunday kept, a rung for every time they held their temper when they had every right to lose it. Some men quit climbing and call it peace. Others climb harder every year and call it faith.

So you climb. Some years you get a few rungs up and feel close. Then the phone gets picked up too late at night, or the grudge against your brother comes back up, or you say the thing at supper you swore you would not say, and you are on the ground again with splinters in your hands. The rungs you built were never as strong as they looked. The dust tells you the trouble is your climbing. Climb better. Build stronger. Try again Monday. And somewhere under all that climbing is a man who is very tired.

That lie has a second half: that God is up there, out of sight, and does not know your name. Bring both halves to the One who does. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) His word in this passage ends the ladder you have been building. A man under a fig tree finds out he was seen before he was called, and then hears Jesus promise heaven opened — opened on the Son of Man Himself.

sections.heading: Found by the Jordan
pulls: The dust hands you a ladder and tells you to climb. Jesus tells a man under a fig tree that heaven stands open — and that the way up is not a thing you build but a Man you follow.
paras: The passage picks up the day after John pointed at the Lamb. Again, the next day, John was standing with two of his disciples, and he says it a second time. This time two men leave John and go after Jesus. By the end of the chapter there are five: Andrew and an unnamed companion, then Simon, then Philip, then Nathanael. None of them knew that morning where the day would end. It is the first small band of the men who will carry this Gospel to the world.

Watch one verb. Found runs through these verses like a rope passed from hand to hand. Andrew finds his brother. Jesus finds Philip. Philip finds Nathanael. But read closely and you will see who does the first finding. Every man in this chapter who comes to Jesus comes because Jesus first turned, first called, first saw. Read 1:35–51 through before you go further, and count the times Jesus moves first. The chapter is a chain of men handing one another to Christ, but the first link is His hand, not theirs.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WHAT ARE YOU LOOKING FOR
paras: John says it again: Behold, the Lamb of God. Nothing more. And the two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus. No preacher was ever handed better proof that he had done his work. His own men walk away from him toward Christ, and John does not call them back. That is what a true witness wants. He wants to be left behind.

Then Jesus does a thing that should stop you where you stand. Jesus turned and saw them following. He does not make them run Him down. The Lord of glory stops for two men who have not yet said a word to Him. He stops on the road, turns around, and asks the question every man has to answer sooner or later: What are you looking for?

Sit with that. Some men come to Jesus looking for a steadier marriage, a cooler temper, a way through a hard year. Some come for the habit, or for their wife’s sake, or because their father did. Jesus does not shame them for it. He asks, because He means to give them more than they came for. And the two men answer with a question of their own, the right one: Rabbi — where are you staying? They do not want a lesson to take home. They want to be where He is.

His answer is the title of this week. Come, and see. Not a reading list. Not a set of terms. An open door and a place at His side. They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. The verb for staying here will come back again and again in this Gospel, until Jesus says, Remain in me, and I in you. The first thing Jesus gives a man is not a task. It is His company.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WE HAVE FOUND THE MESSIAH
paras: One of the two is named: Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. And the first thing Andrew does after a day with Jesus is go looking for family. He first found his own brother, Simon, and told him, We have found the Messiah.

Andrew does not preach at Simon. He does not argue him into anything. He tells him what he found, and then he brought him to Jesus. That is the whole of Andrew’s method, and it has never needed improving: one man who has sat with Jesus, walking his brother up the road to Him. Simon did not come because Andrew was clever. He came because Andrew had been with Jesus and could not keep it to himself.

Then Jesus does what only God does. Jesus looked at him, and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas”. He looks at a fisherman and names him. He names who Simon is — his father’s son — and who Simon will be. The new name is not earned and not bargained for. It is spoken over him before he has done one thing to live up to it, the way God once renamed Abram and Jacob.

The same Lord looks at you. He knows the name your father gave you and every name the dust has given you since. And He has a name for you that you did not earn. This Gospel has already told you what it is: to those who believe in his name, He gave the right to become God’s children. You do not get the new name by becoming a better man. You become a new man because He has already looked at you and spoken.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: UNDER THE FIG TREE
pulls: Jacob saw a stairway in a dream and woke up afraid. Jesus tells you the stairway is a Man, that heaven stands open on Him, and that a son of Jacob can come in by Him without fear.
paras: On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Read that slowly. Philip did not find Jesus. Jesus went and found Philip, and said two words that have been reaching men ever since: Follow me.

Philip runs to Nathanael with news too big to keep: We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, wrote. Notice who Philip says did the finding. The writer has just told you who found whom. A man found by Christ will often talk as if he did the finding, and Christ lets him. Then Philip adds the detail that nearly sinks it: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. Nathanael has his answer ready. Can any good thing come out of Nazareth? He is not wicked for asking. He is honest, and Jesus can work with honest.

Philip does not argue. Come and see. And as Nathanael comes, Jesus speaks first: Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit. Nathanael is caught flat. How do you know me? Jesus answers, Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.

That sentence undoes him. The text does not say what happened under that tree, and you do not need it to. Jesus was there before Philip was, and saw. You have a fig tree of your own — the place you go when no one is watching. The cab at lunch with the radio off. The porch after the house is asleep. Jesus saw you there before anyone called you to Him. He has seen the whole of you, and He has not turned away. That is not a threat. It is the best news a hiding man can hear.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: HEAVEN OPENED
paras: Nathanael’s doubt breaks all at once. Rabbi, you are the Son of God — and more, King of Israel. The man who sneered at Nazareth a few verses back now says more about Jesus than anyone has said all day, and he says it on the strength of one sentence about a tree. Jesus does not tell him he has gone too far. He tells him he has hardly started: You will see greater things than these.

Then He says it — and He says I tell you all, so the promise is not for Nathanael alone — with the solemn opening He saves for what He most wants a man to hear: Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.

Those words come from Genesis. Jacob, the cheat, was running from the brother he had robbed. He lay down with a stone under his head, and he dreamed and saw a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven, with angels going up and down. He woke afraid and said, This is none other than God’s house, and this is the gate of heaven.

Now Jesus says the angels go up and down on the Son of Man. He is the stairway. The gate of heaven is not a spot on a map. It is a Man. You do not build the way up to God. The way up came down — the Son of Man who descended out of heaven — and He is the only way there is. Heaven is not shut to the man who comes to Jesus. In Him it stands open, and it stays open. Every man who comes by Him comes all the way in.

stations.verse: The two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus.
stations.question: Two men heard John’s word about the Lamb and followed Jesus, and He turned and asked them, What are you looking for? If He asked me that on the road today, what would my true answer be?
stations.live: Pick one stretch this week — the drive in, the walk to the barn — and spend it with Jesus as company, not as a chore. Read 1:35–39 first. Then say it: ‘You know me. I’m coming after You.’
body: Akoloutheō means to accompany, to follow — plain road language for walking behind someone who is going somewhere. It is also used of following as a disciple. Eighty-six New Testament verses use it, eighteen of them in John’s Gospel.

The two men in 1:37 follow on foot, down a road by the Jordan. The same verb comes back near the Gospel’s end, when Jesus tells Peter, You follow me. In between, Jesus ties promises to it: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and He who follows me will not walk in the darkness.
