The dust says following is a test of stamina — keep up or be left behind. But look at the order in 10:27. He knows them first. The sheep follow a Shepherd who already has them, and no one snatches them out of His hand. Following is what a known man does with his feet.

stations.verse: He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
stations.question: After one afternoon with Jesus, Andrew first found his own brother, Simon, and told him plainly, We have found the Messiah; what keeps me from telling someone in my own family what I have found in Christ?
stations.live: Tell one person in your family this week, in a sentence, what you have found in Jesus. Do not polish it. Andrew did not. ‘I have found the One God promised. Come and see Him.’
body: Messias is a Greek spelling of an Aramaic word that matches the Hebrew mashiach, and it means the same as Christos — one title in two tongues. In the whole New Testament it appears only twice, both times in John: on Andrew’s lips here, and on the lips of a Samaritan woman at a well.

Both times the Greek title follows at once — here, which is, being interpreted, Christ, and at the well, he who is called Christ. No reader is left outside. Andrew uses the old word, full of the hope of Israel, and John hands it to every reader in a word he can understand. The One God promised has come, and He is for Galilean fishermen, for Samaritan women, and for you.

The dust says the promises of God are for men further along than you. Messias says the Promised One walked up a riverbank and let two strangers spend the rest of the day with Him. He is not waiting for you to qualify. He has already come.

stations.verse: Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said about him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!
stations.question: Nathanael said bluntly what he thought of Nazareth, and Jesus called him an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit; where am I keeping up a front with God instead of bringing Him my real doubts and sins?
stations.gloss: an Israelite; a name carrying the privilege of God’s people
stations.live: Find one place you are shading the truth — the timesheet, the tax form, the story you tell at home. Bring it into the open this week: ‘Lord, You saw it already. I’m done hiding it.’
body: Israēlitēs means an Israelite, and the name itself speaks of privilege — belonging to the people God claimed. Paul lists what came with it: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service, and the promises.

The name goes back to a man who did not deserve it. Jacob came with deceit and took his brother’s blessing, and God named him Israel anyway. Now Jesus looks at one of Jacob’s sons and calls him an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit.

The dust says you are your worst angle — the deal you shaded, the story you trimmed. Jesus sees through every angle, and still He calls. David knew where a straight heart comes from: Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity, in whose spirit there is no deceit. Forgiveness comes first. Honesty grows in it.

stations.verse: Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.
stations.question: Jesus told Nathanael, Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you; what changes for me if Christ saw me in my most hidden place before I came, and called me anyway?
stations.live: Go to your own fig tree this week — the place where you are most alone. Sit there five minutes and say it: ‘You saw me here before I came to You. You see me now.’
body: Sykē is a fig tree, no more and no less. Fifteen New Testament verses mention it. John uses it only in this scene, twice: once when Jesus tells Nathanael where He saw him, and again when He repeats it back to him.

The text does not say what Nathanael was doing under that tree, and you should not guess. What it says is enough: when you were under the fig tree, I saw you. Before Philip called and before Nathanael had one thought of coming, Jesus already had His eyes on him. It is the same order as the father in Luke, who saw his son while he was still far off.

The dust tells you the private places are where God is not. That is backward. The hidden place is exactly where Jesus says, I saw you — and the eyes that saw you there are the eyes that called you out.

stations.verse: He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
stations.question: Jesus promised His new followers they would see the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man, Himself the stairway Jacob dreamed of; what rung am I still building to reach God on my own?
stations.gloss: a messenger; an angel, one sent from God
stations.live: When you pray this week, start by naming the way in: ‘I come through Jesus. Heaven is open on Him.’ Then pray as a man walking through an open door, not as one pounding on a locked one.
body: Angelos means a messenger, one sent. From there it takes its special sense of angel: a heavenly being who attends on God and is sent either to make His purposes known or to carry them out. It runs through a hundred and seventy-one verses of the New Testament, but John’s Gospel uses it in only three.

In 1:51 they go ascending and descending on the Son of Man — Jacob’s stairway, with Jesus Himself in the place of the stairs. In 20:12 two of them sit in the empty tomb where the body of Jesus had lain. All the traffic between heaven and earth runs on Him, and the empty grave shows the way is clear.

The dust says heaven sends word only to better men. Jesus says heaven is opened on Him, and that there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting. The open heaven is not reserved for the clean. It is opened for sinners who come by Him.

practices.title: ANSWER HIS QUESTION
practices.body: Jesus asked two men, What are you looking for? Write your own answer on the back of an envelope and keep it on the dash. If the true answer is a better year, a calmer house, or a fix for your temper, write that down. Then read 1:38–39 and let Jesus answer you the way He answered them: Come, and see. He gives Himself before He gives anything else. Keep the envelope, and read it again on Friday to see what He has given.

practices.title: STAY WITH HIM A WHILE
practices.body: Two men stayed with Jesus that day, and it was the first thing they did as His followers. Set aside one long stretch this week — a Saturday morning, an evening with the television off — and read John 1 straight through, slowly, twice. No list of questions. No plan to get something out of it. If your mind wanders, start the chapter over. Let the phone sit in another room. He has opened His door to you. Stay where He is.

practices.title: BRING ONE BROTHER
practices.body: Andrew found his own brother first and brought him. Name one man — a brother, a son, a man at the shop — who needs to meet Jesus. Pray for him by name each day before you ever say a word to him. Then before the week is out, say one plain sentence to him: ‘I have found Someone. Come and see.’ You are not responsible for what Jesus says to him next. Andrew only brought Simon. Jesus did the naming.

practices.title: COME OUT FROM UNDER THE TREE
practices.body: Jesus saw Nathanael where no one else did. Name the private place where you go to hide — the phone at night, the bottle in the garage, the grudge you rehearse on the drive home. Tell God plainly what happens there. The One who saw you there is the One who bore it on the cross. He saw it before you ever called on Him, and He still calls you. Then tell one trusted brother, so the hiding place has some daylight in it. Hiding loses its grip in daylight.

practices.title: PRAY THROUGH THE OPEN DOOR
practices.body: Heaven is opened on the Son of Man. Each morning this week, before you ask for anything, say: ‘I come to You through Jesus, the way You opened.’ Then pray plainly, as a son who has been let in, the way a man walks into his own father’s house. On the days you feel shut out, read 1:51 again. The door does not swing with your feelings. It hangs on Christ, and He does not move.

title: Come and See
subtitle: from dust to the open heaven
keyVerse: He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.

passage.text: Again, the next day, John was standing with two of his disciples,
and he looked at Jesus as he walked, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!”
The two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus.
Jesus turned and saw them following, and said to them, “What are you looking for?” They said to him, “Rabbi” (which is to say, being interpreted, Teacher), “where are you staying?”
He said to them, “Come, and see.” They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.
One of the two who heard John and followed him was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.
He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him, and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter).
On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, of the city of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”
Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and said about him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!”
Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are King of Israel!”
Jesus answered him, “Because I told you, ‘I saw you underneath the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these!”
He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE OPEN HEAVEN
stationsIntro: Take these five words slowly, one a morning if you can. Each one shows a man being found by Jesus before he knew he was looking.
lifeIntro: Jesus moved first in every scene of this passage. He turned, He called, He saw, He named, and He promised an open heaven on Himself. None of what follows earns you a way in. Each practice is a step through a door He has already opened.
lifePulls: Jesus turned on the road and asked two men what they were looking for. He found Philip, saw Nathanael, and named Simon. Every man in this chapter who came to Him had already been found.
prayer: Father, You opened heaven, and You opened it on Your Son. Jesus turned toward me before I knew I was looking for Him. He saw me under my own fig tree, and He did not walk away. Forgive me for trying to reach You by my own strength. Thank You for the new name I did not earn. Give me a plain tongue to say to my brother, Come and see. When I hide under my own tree, call me out by name. Keep me following, close enough to hear His voice. Let me live this week as a man let in through the open door. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You opened heaven, and You opened it on Your Son.
Jesus turned toward me before I knew I was looking for Him.
He saw me under my own fig tree, and He did not walk away.
Forgive me for trying to reach You by my own strength.
Thank You for the new name I did not earn.
Give me a plain tongue to say to my brother, Come and see.
When I hide under my own tree, call me out by name.
Keep me following, close enough to hear His voice.
Let me live this week as a man let in through the open door.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus moved first. He turned and asked two men what they were looking for. He found Philip. He saw Nathanael under the fig tree before anyone called him. He has already seen you. Then He told them heaven stood open — on Him. The dust hands you a ladder and tells you to climb. Put it down. The way to God is a Man, and He says to you what He said by the Jordan: Come and see.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, you who were seen before you ever looked up. He saw two men behind Him on the road, and He turned. He saw Simon, and He gave him a new name. He saw Philip, and He went out to find him. He saw Nathanael under the fig tree before anyone called his name. And He has seen you — at the shop, in the cab, on the porch after dark — and He has come down the road toward you anyway.

You have been building ladders. A rung of church attendance, a rung of a cleaner month, a rung of doing better than your father did. And every time you got a few rungs up, the dust pulled you down again. The ladder was never the way. Jacob never climbed his stairway. He lay on the bare ground with a stone under his head, a cheat on the run, and God came down to him and said, I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go. Jacob was not a better man when he woke. He was a seen man and a promised man.

Jesus is that stairway, and He did not stay at the top. The Word came down into the dust. He was lifted up on a cross, and every angle and lie you ever worked was laid on Him there. Then the stone was taken from His tomb, and two angels sat where His body had lain, and heaven stood open to every man who comes in His name. The gate of heaven is a Man with nail scars in His hands. No one goes up but the One who came down — and He carries you up in Himself.

So come and see. Go to work this week as a man for whom heaven is not a locked building. You were seen before you were called. You were called before you followed. And the One you follow has promised you greater things than these: heaven opened on the Son of Man, and you, a son of Jacob’s kind, let in by Him and kept by Him wherever you go. When the dust tells you next Monday that the door has swung shut again, answer it with His own words: hereafter you will see heaven opened.
closingVerse: He said to him, “Most certainly, I tell you all, hereafter you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
carry: Jesus promises you will see heaven opened on the Son of Man, not at the top of a ladder you build; what would it look like for you to come to God this week through Him alone?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust has a theory about joy. It runs out. You got the good years first — the strong back, the young wife, the first paycheck that felt bigger than it was — and now you are drinking what is left at the bottom of the barrel. Your knees tell you so every morning. The bills on the counter agree with them. Even the old songs sound thinner than they used to.

Men carry that theory into church without knowing it. They figure God works the way every other host works: the good stuff first, the cheap stuff later, once nobody is paying attention. Grace was strong at the start, back when you first believed. Now it runs thin. Now you live on whatever you can still squeeze out of duty and habit. You still go. You still give. But you expect less of God every year, and you call that growing up.

The dust says your best is behind you and God is rationing what remains. A man who believes that will lie down in it and call it realism. He stops asking God for much, because he has decided there is not much left to give. But there is another prayer for a man in that place: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) He is asking for more than leftovers. At a village wedding in Galilee, Jesus answers him with six stone jars and a verdict from the man in charge of the feast: You have kept the good wine until now.

sections.heading: The Beginning of His Signs
pulls: The dust says God serves the good wine first and spends the rest of your life pouring out what is left. At Cana the ruler of the feast said the opposite — and he had tasted it.
paras: John does not call this a miracle. He calls it a sign — the first of them — and at the end of his book he tells you why he wrote any of them down: that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. A sign points past itself. The wine at Cana was real wine, poured into real cups at a real wedding. But John wants your eyes on the One who made it. Every sign in this book is a finger, and every finger points to Jesus.

The scene is small: a village called Cana, a wedding where the wine fails, a mother who notices, servants who haul water, and a ruler of the feast who never learns where the best wine came from. There is no crowd and no sermon. Only the servants who drew the water knew what had happened, and the disciples who watched. Read John 2:1–12 through twice before you go further, and watch how quietly the Son of God shows His glory.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE WINE RAN OUT
paras: The third day, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there. Then John adds a line you might skip: Jesus also was invited, with his disciples, to the wedding. The Word who was with God in the beginning, through whom all things were made, accepted an invitation to a village feast. He came. He sat down among farmers and fishermen and somebody’s cousins. He was not too holy for a wedding, and He is not too holy for your table. The first thing John shows you after the testimony of chapter one is Jesus at a party, among people glad to be together.

Then the trouble: When the wine ran out. John gives no reason. He does not say who planned badly or who drank too much. The wine simply ran out, the way things in this world run out. Wages run out before the month does. Strength runs out before the job is done. Patience runs out somewhere around the third time your son ignores you. Every man knows the sound of a pump sucking air. You can feel it in the bottom of your chest on a Sunday night, when the week ahead looks longer than what you have left in you.

Jesus’ mother sees it, and she does one thing. She brings it to Him. They have no wine. Four words. No speech, no plan, no list of what He ought to do about it. She names the empty thing and sets it in front of Him. That is about as plain as prayer gets, and it is a good pattern for a man who thinks he has to have the answer worked out before he is allowed to ask.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: MY HOUR HAS NOT YET COME
paras: His answer sounds hard at first. Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come. Jesus is not on anyone’s schedule — not the bridegroom’s, not His disciples’, not even His mother’s. That is not coldness. It is the Son keeping step with His Father, the way He will keep step all the way to the end. He answers to His Father. Whatever He does at Cana, He will do because it is His to do, and not because anyone pushed Him into it.

Keep your eye on that word hour. It runs all through John like a thread through a sack. Men will try to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come (7:30). Later He will say, The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified (12:23), and He will mean the cross. Every sign He gives points toward that hour. Cana is a small window. Golgotha is the open door. The wine at the wedding is a first taste of what His hour will pour out for the whole world.

His mother does not argue. She turns to the servants and says, Whatever he says to you, do it. Then she says nothing more. Her last word here points away from herself and toward her Son. That is the right place for anyone’s word to point. The servants are left with Jesus and whatever He tells them, which is exactly where you are left this week. You will not get the whole plan. You will get His word, and the word will be enough to start walking.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: FILLED TO THE BRIM
pulls: The servants carried water because He told them to. Somewhere between the jar and the ruler’s cup it became wine. You do not have to understand the change to carry what He hands you.
paras: John slows down to show you the jars. Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying. He tells you what they were for. They held water for washing — water for the outside of a man, for making him clean. They were large, set in place, and someone had to fill them by hand. John does not tell you how long the filling took. He tells you there were six of them, and that they were stone.

Jesus gives the order. Fill the water pots with water. So they filled them up to the brim. Nobody asked why. Nobody filled them halfway to see what would happen first. Then He says, Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast. Think of that walk. A servant carrying a cup of what he had poured in as plain water, toward the man in charge, with no proof in his hand except a word from Jesus. He did not know what he was carrying until somebody tasted it. Most faithful obedience feels like that from the inside. You carry the cup. Somebody else tastes the wine.

What happened in those jars is what happens when Christ comes. John has already told you, For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ (1:17). The law was good, and the washing pointed somewhere. But it could only wash. It could not make a man glad. Christ does not throw the old jars out. He fills them past what they ever held. What the washing promised, He gives.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE GOOD WINE KEPT UNTIL NOW
paras: The ruler of the feast tastes it. He has no idea where it came from, but the servants who had drawn the water knew. Then he calls the bridegroom over and says what every host in the world knows: Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. And then the verdict: You have kept the good wine until now.

That is the world’s way and Christ’s way set side by side. The world pours its best first and leaves you the dregs. Youth, strength, the pleasures of sin — they all taste best at the start and worse every year after. Christ runs the other direction. With Him the life you have now is not a slow slide down from the day you believed. From his fullness we all received grace upon grace (1:16). He keeps the better wine for later. A man in Christ is not drinking the bottom of the barrel. He is a guest at a feast that is still getting better.

Then John tells you what it all meant. This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him. Not that the wedding was saved, though it was, and the feast went on. Not that the bridegroom was spared embarrassment. His glory was shown, and men believed Him. That is the whole aim of the sign. It does not ask you to become a better host. It asks you to believe the One who made the wine, and to keep believing Him on the days when the cupboards at your own house look bare.

stations.verse: The third day, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there.
stations.question: John sets the first of Jesus’ signs not in the temple but at a wedding in Cana of Galilee, among plain people at a feast; what part of my ordinary week have I assumed Jesus has no interest in?
stations.gloss: a wedding; especially a wedding feast
stations.live: This week, accept the next invitation to a family meal or celebration you would rather skip. Go, sit down, and remember who else sat at a wedding: ‘He came to the feast. He is not ashamed to sit at mine.’
body: Gamos means a wedding, and especially the wedding feast — the meal and the celebration, not only the vows. It appears in sixteen New Testament verses, and once, in Hebrews 13:4, it means marriage itself. Jesus uses it in His story of a king who made a wedding feast for his son.

So the word John sets at the start of the signs is the same word Scripture sets at the end of history: the wedding supper of the Lamb. The first sign happens at a wedding feast. The last scene is one. In between, a man can grow suspicious of joy, as though God only meets him in hospital hallways and at gravesides.
The dust says God is grim and faith is a long face. Gamos says the Son of God was invited to a wedding and went. And He is getting another feast ready, with your name on the guest list.

stations.verse: When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.
stations.question: When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother did not fix it or explain it; she said only, They have no wine; what empty thing in my house am I still trying to manage before I bring it to Jesus?
stations.live: Pray one prayer this week with no explaining in it. Name the thing that has run out — patience, money, the warmth in your marriage — and stop there. Say it plainly, the way she did: ‘Lord, I have none left.’
body: Oinos is the plain word for wine. The New Testament uses it in twenty-six verses. Four are in John: three at Cana, and one more when John looks back to the place where he made the water into wine (4:46). Revelation also uses it as a figure, for the wine of the wrath of God (14:10).

Wine at a wedding means the feast goes on. When it runs out, the party is over. That is all Jesus’ mother says to Him. She names the empty thing and brings it to her Son. A man can pray long and say little. She said four words, and they were enough.

The dust says your cup is going dry and God has quit pouring. At Cana He did not ration. Six stone jars, filled to the brim, became wine — more than one village feast could drink. The One who made it has not run short since, and He is not stingy with you.

stations.verse: Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece.
stations.question: The six stone pots stood there after the Jews’ way of purifying, and Jesus filled them with the best wine; what am I still trusting to keep me clean before God instead of the Christ that washing pointed to?
stations.live: Name one way you have tried to wash yourself clean before God — a promise, a streak of good behavior, a hard week of effort. Lay it down at His feet and pray: ‘You fill what I could only wash.’
body: Hydria is built on hydōr, water. It is a water-pot, a jar for holding water, though the word could be used for a jar of any kind. It shows up in only three New Testament verses, all in John: twice at Cana, and once at a well in Samaria, where a woman left her water pot and ran to town.

John tells you what these six jars were for: the Jews’ way of purifying. They held water for washing. They were stone, large and set in place, and men had to fill them by hand. Jesus did not smash them. He had them filled to the brim, and then He changed what was in them.

The dust wants you to keep scrubbing at the outside, trying to get clean enough to be welcome. Jesus brings what the washing water never could. Your jar is not too plain, too cracked, or too old for Him to fill.

stations.verse: He said to them, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” So they took it.
stations.question: Jesus told the servants, Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast, and they carried it before anyone had tasted wine; what plain word of His am I holding back until I see how it turns out?
stations.gloss: the man in charge of a banquet, who arranged the tables and food
stations.live: Do one plain, unseen task this week because Jesus told you to love your neighbor — the dishes, a ride, a repair for the widow down the road. Say it as you go: ‘I carry. He changes it.’
body: Architriklinos is built on triklinos, a dining room with three couches. It names the man in charge of a banquet, whose job was to arrange the tables and the food. The word appears in just two verses of the New Testament, both of them right here. The World English Bible calls him the ruler of the feast.

He ran the feast and missed the miracle. He tasted the wine and didn’t know where it came from. The servants who had drawn the water knew. The man in charge praised the result. The men who obeyed saw where it came from. Being near the work of Jesus has less to do with rank than with doing what He says.

The dust says the men with titles see what God is doing, and you are only carrying water. Cana says the water carriers knew first. Obedience does not earn you the miracle. It puts you close enough to watch Him work.

stations.verse: This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
stations.question: John says the point of Cana was not a rescued party but that Jesus revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him; what does the good wine show me about Jesus that I need to trust Him for this week?
stations.gloss: a sign, mark, token; a miracle as a sign of divine authority
stations.live: Read John 2:1–11 aloud once this week and stop at verse 11. Sit with it a minute. Then say back what the sign showed you: ‘Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. He keeps the good wine until now.’
body: Sēmeion means a sign, a mark, a token — something that marks out a person or thing from all others. It is also used of miracles seen as signs of divine authority. John has it in seventeen verses, out of sixty-nine across the New Testament.

John chose the word on purpose. He does not need you to gasp. He needs you to look where the sign points. At Cana it points to glory: Jesus revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him. At the end of the book John says the signs he chose are written, that you may believe.

The dust wants a sign that settles your doubts on your own terms. John hands you a finished set of them, and the first one is sitting in stone jars full of wine. The sign has been given. What is left for you is to believe Him and live.

practices.title: NAME THE EMPTY JAR
practices.body: His mother said four words: They have no wine. Write down plainly what has run out in your life — money, strength, the warmth at home, the joy you once had in Christ. Do not dress it up or explain it. Each morning this week, bring that one line to Jesus and leave it in front of Him. You are not asking Him to follow your plan. You are naming the empty thing to the One who fills. That is faith, even when it feels like nothing more than honesty.

practices.title: DO WHAT HE SAYS
practices.body: Whatever he says to you, do it. Pick one plain word of Jesus you already know and have been putting off — forgive the man who cheated you, speak gently to your wife, stop the side comment at the shop. Do it this week before you see how it turns out. The servants poured water and carried a cup with nothing in hand but His word. That is enough to go on. Obedience before sight is not blind. It is trust in the One who spoke.

practices.title: FILL IT TO THE BRIM
practices.body: The servants did not fill the jars halfway to test Him. Where have you been giving Christ a half measure — a verse in a hurry, a prayer on the way out the door? This week read one whole chapter of John each morning before work, slowly, with your coffee going cold. Fill the jar. Then let Him do with it what only He can do. The filling is your part. The changing is His, and He has never once failed to do it.

practices.title: COUNT WHAT HE HAS KEPT
practices.body: The dust says your best years are behind you. Write down three graces you have now that you did not have ten years ago — a sin that has lost its grip, a friend in Christ, a truth you finally understand. Tape it inside a cabinet door. Read the list when the dust starts talking. Christ keeps the good wine for later, and what you hold today is not leftovers. Thank Him for each line by name before you go to bed.

practices.title: GO TO THE FEAST
practices.body: Jesus was invited, and He went. Say yes to one meal or gathering this week that you would usually dodge — the cookout, the birthday, the supper after church — and sit at the table without checking your phone. And come to the Lord’s Table at your church with your eyes open. He feeds His people there, and the meal points ahead to the feast He has promised. Take the bread and the cup as a man who has been invited, not a man sneaking in.

title: Water into Wine
subtitle: from dust to the good wine kept until now
keyVerse: This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.

passage.text: The third day, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there.
Jesus also was invited, with his disciples, to the wedding.
When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.”
Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come.”
His mother said to the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it.”
Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece.
Jesus said to them, “Fill the water pots with water.” So they filled them up to the brim.
He said to them, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” So they took it.
When the ruler of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and didn’t know where it came from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the ruler of the feast called the bridegroom
and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!”
This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
After this, he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples; and they stayed there a few days.

stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly and let it settle before you answer. These five words come straight from the wedding at Cana, and each one points past the feast to the One who kept the good wine until now.
lifeIntro: Jesus has already done the work at Cana. He filled the jars, changed the water, and showed His glory, and His disciples believed. None of that waited on you. These five practices are ways of bringing your empty jars to the One who fills them, and of doing what He says while you wait to taste it.
lifePulls: The world pours its best first and leaves you the dregs. Christ does it the other way around. Whatever you have tasted of His grace so far, He has kept better for later, and He has never once run short.
prayer: Father, thank You for sending Your Son to a wedding in Cana. Thank You that He did not stand off from the tables of ordinary men but sat down at them. I have run out of more than wine — strength, patience, joy, the will to keep going. I name the empty jars to You plainly, and I leave them with Your Son. Make me quick to do whatever He says, even before I see what He will do. Keep me from believing the lie that my best days with You are behind me. Show me His glory in Your word this week, and make me believe Him. Thank You that He drank the cup of wrath so I could drink the good wine. Keep me looking ahead to the feast Your Son has promised. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, thank You for sending Your Son to a wedding in Cana.
Thank You that He did not stand off from the tables of ordinary men but sat down at them.
I have run out of more than wine — strength, patience, joy, the will to keep going.
I name the empty jars to You plainly, and I leave them with Your Son.
Make me quick to do whatever He says, even before I see what He will do.
Keep me from believing the lie that my best days with You are behind me.
Show me His glory in Your word this week, and make me believe Him.
Thank You that He drank the cup of wrath so I could drink the good wine.
Keep me looking ahead to the feast Your Son has promised.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: The wine ran out at a village wedding, and Jesus turned six jars of washing water into the best wine of the night. John calls it the first sign: it showed His glory, and His disciples believed Him. The dust says God pours the good wine first and gives you thinner stuff every year after. Christ does the opposite. Name the empty jar, do whatever He says, and expect better wine ahead, because the Bridegroom has kept it.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the One who sat down at a wedding. Lift them to the One who heard four plain words about wine that had run out and did not turn away. Lift them to the One who told tired servants to fill heavy jars to the brim, and then made water into wine without lifting a cup Himself. Lift them to the One who let the servants know what the man in charge never found out. Lift them higher still, to the One who has kept the good wine until now.

The dust told you that joy runs out and God rations what is left. It told you that the start of your faith was the high-water mark and the rest is a slow leak. But the ruler of the feast tasted the wine and said the last pour was the best. He did not know where it came from. You do. It came from the hands of Jesus Christ, who was in the beginning with God and was God, and who took on flesh and walked into a village wedding. The same hands are not empty toward you now.

And it cost Him more than it cost the servants. The wine at Cana was free to the guests. The cup Jesus took in the garden was not free to Him. He said, The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it? — and He drank it down to the last of the wrath you had coming. His hour came, and He went to it on purpose, so that not one drop of that judgment would be left for you. He finished it.

So hold on to this when the week runs dry. There is a wedding feast ahead that no sin, no grave, and no lean season can cancel. John was told to write it down: Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb. If you belong to Christ, you are invited. The Bridegroom has kept the good wine for that day. Everything you taste of Him now — every answered prayer, every forgiven morning, every sin that loosens its grip — is a sip before the feast. The best is still in the jars.
closingVerse: This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
carry: At Cana Jesus revealed his glory by serving the best wine last; where have you quietly decided that your best days with Him are behind you?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust will let you keep your religion. It only asks you to run it like a store. You pay in, God pays out. A Sunday in the pew, a check in the plate, a clean month with the bottle or the screen — each one a coin slid across the counter. Then, when trouble comes, you pull out your receipts and wonder why the store is not honoring them. You did your part. Where is His?

It is an easy lie to live inside, because it feels like faithfulness. You are there. You are giving. You are trying. But the whole time your eyes are on what you will walk out with. God becomes the supplier and you become the customer, and the relationship lasts exactly as long as the deal keeps paying. When it stops paying, a man either works harder or quits coming. Both of those are the same mistake. Both of them think God can be bought.

Standing with God, the dust tells you, is bought in small change, and every man keeps his own ledger. Run that ledger long enough and you will end up face down, out of coin, with nothing left in the drawer but one honest prayer: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The word that revives him in John 2 does not come gently. It comes with a whip of cords, a pile of coins on the stone floor, and a promise about a temple that would be torn down and raised again.

sections.heading: Passover in Jerusalem
pulls: The dust says God runs a store and you are paying off your account in small change. Jesus walked into the market with a whip of cords and poured the coins on the floor.
paras: John moves you from a village wedding to the center of the nation. The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Passover was the feast of the lamb, and John has already let you hear John the Baptist cry out, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. Now the Lamb walks into His Father’s house at Passover, and He does not like what He finds. At the feast that remembered God’s rescue, He finds a market.

The passage turns on one hinge. In the first half Jesus cleans the temple. In the second half He tells you that He Himself is the temple. Read John 2:13–25 twice before you go on. Watch His hands in the first half and His words in the second, and notice what the disciples did not understand until after He was raised from the dead. They stood in those courts and saw it all, and still missed the point for years. You have the end of the story already in your hands. Read it that way.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A MARKET IN THE HOUSE
paras: He found in the temple those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and the changers of money sitting. John does not explain how their trade worked or how it got there. He tells you what Jesus found. Livestock, cages, coin. And men sitting — settled in, comfortable, open for business, as though they belonged there and always would. Nobody looked surprised to see them.

The house built for the worship of God had become a place where lovers of money took the room meant for lovers of God. Worship still happened there. Sacrifices were still offered. But the noise of trade had crowded into the place of prayer, and nobody seemed to mind. That is what makes it so dangerous. A market in the house of God rarely looks like rebellion. It looks like business as usual.

Before you shake your head at them, look at your own house. A man can keep every outward form of worship and still have tables set up inside. The phone that sits closer to him than his Bible. The money that gets the first and best of his thinking. The grudge he tends like a side business. Nobody hauled those tables in on one morning. They came in one at a time, each with a good reason, and he got used to the noise. After a while he could not hear it anymore.

John gives you this scene early for a reason. The first thing Jesus does in Jerusalem is walk into the center of Israel’s worship and look at it with His Father’s eyes. He still does that, in every heart He means to live in.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A WHIP OF CORDS
paras: He made a whip of cords, and threw all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the changers’ money and overthrew their tables. Read the first verb again. He made it. He did not grab the nearest stick in a flash of temper. He took cords and twisted them into a tool, and then He used it. This was zeal with its mind made up. Anger that flares and fades is common in men. This was something steadier, and it came from love for His Father’s name.

Men like a mild Jesus — one who smiles, nods, and never upsets the arrangement. Men also fear an angry Jesus who is looking for a reason to strike. John gives you neither. He gives you the Son, clearing His Father’s house of what did not belong in it, with the same hands that would later be nailed down for the people who had filled it.

Then He speaks to the dove sellers: Take these things out of here. Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace. Listen to the claim inside that sentence: My Father’s house. Only a Son talks that way. He has come home and found His Father’s house full of merchants, and He will not leave them there.

That is good news, though it does not sound like it at first. The Son does not leave His Father’s house the way He found it. He does not leave yours that way either. If He has begun to turn over tables in you — to make you sick of the trade you once made peace with — that is not a sign He has turned against you. It is a sign the Son has come home.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ZEAL THAT ATE HIM UP
pulls: The zeal that turned over the tables did not stop at the temple steps. It carried Jesus to the cross and ate Him up there. His zeal was not first aimed at you. It was spent for you.
paras: His disciples remembered that it was written: Zeal for your house will eat me up. They reached back to Psalm 69, a psalm of a righteous man suffering for God’s sake. The next line of that verse says, The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me. The zeal that cleared the market would cost Jesus everything. Men would hate Him for it. Their contempt for God would land on Him. The disciples did not yet know how far that would go.

Follow that psalm a little further and you find another line: In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink. Now turn to the end of John’s Gospel. On the cross Jesus says, I am thirsty. A sponge full of vinegar is lifted to His mouth. When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished. The zeal that overturned tables in chapter two ate Him up on a Roman cross. He was consumed — not by a mob’s rage only, but by His own love for the Father and for the people the Father had given Him.

So when you read about the whip, do not stop there. A man who sees only the whip will either hide from Jesus or try to get on His good side by cleaning up. Neither one is faith. His zeal was not first aimed at you. It was spent for you. The One who burned to see His Father’s house made clean went to the cross to make a dirty people clean enough to live in it. He paid for the cleaning Himself, in His own body, and He did not send you the bill.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: DESTROY THIS TEMPLE
paras: The leaders want proof. What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things? Jesus answers, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. They hear stone. It took forty-six years to build this temple, they say. Will you raise it up in three days? But John tells you, he spoke of the temple of his body. The true meeting place of God and man was standing in front of them in flesh and bone.

They did tear it down. And He raised it, just as He said. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he said this, and they believed the Scripture, and the word which Jesus had said. The empty tomb made sense of what had puzzled them. It will do the same for you. Many words of Jesus that confuse you now will open up when you read them in the light of the resurrection.

Then John closes with a warning and a comfort. Many believed in his name, observing his signs. But Jesus didn’t entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone. He was not impressed by a crowd. He himself knew what was in man. He knows what is in you — every table you have let in, every coin you have counted — and He did not stay away. He went into death with that knowledge and came out of the grave still holding on to His own. A Savior who knows the worst and keeps you anyway is the only kind worth trusting. You can stop hiding the tables. He has already seen them, and He is still the One who came to clear them out.

stations.verse: He found in the temple those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and the changers of money sitting.
stations.question: When Jesus came up at Passover He found in the temple men selling and changing money, sitting there as if they belonged; what has settled into my worship so long that I no longer notice it, though He does?
stations.live: Watch for the moment this week when you start adding up what God owes you for your faithfulness. Stop counting right there, at the sink or the gas pump, and say it plainly: ‘I am not buying anything. I was bought.’
body: Kermatistēs comes from a verb, kermatizō, to cut small, to change money into small coin. The kermatistēs is a money changer — a man who deals in small change. The word appears only once in the New Testament, right here, of the men Jesus found sitting in His Father’s house.

John does not tell you how their trade worked, and you do not need him to. He tells you where they sat. Men still sit there. The coin is smaller now — an hour in a pew, a check in the plate, a stretch of good behavior — pushed across the counter with the same hope: that God will owe you.

The dust says standing with God is bought a little at a time, in small change. Jesus poured the coins out on the ground. Your standing was bought once, by Him, with a price you could never have counted out. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price.

stations.verse: He made a whip of cords, and threw all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the changers’ money and overthrew their tables.
stations.question: Jesus did not ask the traders to tidy up; He threw all out of the temple and overturned their tables; what in me am I asking Him to manage politely that I need to let Him clear out?
stations.live: When you picture Jesus this week, picture both scenes: the whip in His hand and the stripes on His back. Then pray: ‘You were zealous for Your Father’s house, and You were flogged for me.’
body: Phragellion is borrowed from the Latin flagellum, a scourge. It appears nowhere else in the New Testament. John says Jesus made a whip of cords. He did not snatch one up. He made it — took the cords and twisted them into a tool before He used it.

That is not a temper flaring. It is zeal with a plan. Men picture Jesus as soft, or they picture Him as harsh, and both pictures miss Him. He drove the merchants and their animals, the sheep and the oxen, out of His Father’s house because the house was His Father’s, and He would not leave it in their hands.

The dust wants you to believe His zeal is aimed at you — the whip lifted over your head, waiting for one more failure. But keep reading John. So Pilate then took Jesus, and flogged him. The One who carried the whip in the temple took the scourge on His own back.

stations.verse: To those who sold the doves, he said, “Take these things out of here! Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace!
stations.question: Jesus called the temple my Father’s house and would not let it become a marketplace; where has my praying or giving turned into a deal with God rather than a son coming to his Father?
stations.gloss: a trading place; an exchange; a market
stations.live: Before worship this Sunday, write down what you were hoping to get out of it. Cross it out before you leave the house. Then pray as you walk in: ‘I came to meet You, not to make a deal.’
body: Emporion is a trading place, an exchange — a place where goods change hands. Jesus says, Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace, and this is the only time the New Testament uses the word. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Ezekiel 27:3, where the prophet speaks against Tyre, the merchant of the peoples.

A market runs on exchange. You give, you get, and both sides keep accounts. That works fine at the feed store. It ruins a house of worship. When a man comes to God to trade, his eyes stay on what he will carry out the door, not on the One he came to meet.

The dust says God is a merchant and grace wears a price tag. But Jesus calls it my Father’s house. In a house there is a Father and a Son, not a seller and a buyer. Through the Son you come in as family, not as a customer.

stations.verse: His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will eat me up.
stations.question: Watching Him clear the temple, His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will eat me up.”; what does it mean for me that the zeal which overturned those tables finally consumed Jesus on the cross?
stations.live: Name one argument this week where your heat was really for your own house. Let it go before supper, and if you owe somebody a word, say it. Then pray: ‘Your zeal was spent on me. Spend mine on Your house.’
body: Zēlos means zeal, and it can also mean jealousy. The one word carries both a burning devotion and a burning envy. It appears in sixteen New Testament verses. Paul uses it of a godly jealousy over the church, and of men who have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

The disciples watched the tables go over and remembered the psalm: Zeal for your house will eat me up. Jesus’ zeal ran toward His Father’s house. A man’s zeal tends to run toward his own — his name, his rights, the last word in the argument. That kind of zeal sours into jealousy fast, and James names what grows from it.

The dust says nothing in you burns for God, so you may as well burn for yourself. But Christ’s zeal ate Him up at the cross for you, before yours ever woke. New zeal is lit from His, not wrung out of you.

stations.verse: Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.
stations.question: Asked for a sign, Jesus pointed to His own body: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up; where am I still demanding some other proof from God when He has already given me the empty tomb?
stations.gloss: to loose, unbind; to break up, destroy
stations.live: Look at the thing in your life that has been torn down — a marriage strained thin, health that will not come back, a name that got ruined. Bring it to Him by name: ‘You were broken down and raised. Loose me.’
body: Lyō means to loose or unbind, and from there to break a thing into its parts — to dissolve, break up, destroy. It appears in thirty-nine New Testament verses. John uses it of a sandal strap (1:27), of the Scripture that can’t be broken (10:35), and at Lazarus’ grave: Free him, and let him go. Here it is the command, Destroy this temple.

Jesus told His enemies the worst thing they would do to Him, and promised what He would do after. They would break down His body. He would raise it up. Acts 2:24 uses the same word for what God did with death itself: He freed him from the agony of death.

The dust says what is broken stays broken. Lyō says the breaking of His body was the start of your release. The grave could not hold Him, and the grave clothes will not hold you. What He loosed, no one ties back up.

practices.title: CLOSE THE COUNTER
practices.body: Find the deal you have been running with God. Maybe it is church attendance in exchange for a safe family, or giving in exchange for a steady paycheck. Write it down in one sentence. Then cross it out and write under it what Jesus actually did: He poured out the coins and paid for you Himself. Read that line every morning this week before you pray, and pray as a son, not a customer. The account is closed because He settled it.

practices.title: LET HIM TURN OVER A TABLE
practices.body: Ask yourself what has crowded out worship in your own house. The phone at bedtime. The ballgame that ate Sunday. The second drink that ends every evening. Pick one and let Him turn it over this week — put it out of reach, out of the room, out of the schedule. This is not a penance. The Son is clearing His Father’s house, and you are getting out of His way. If you fail on Wednesday, you are still His. Pick it up again Thursday.

practices.title: WORSHIP THE FATHER, NOT THE DEAL
practices.body: Worship goes empty when it turns toward what you want and away from who Jesus is and what He has done. This week, start every prayer by naming something God has done in Christ before you ask for anything — the cross, the empty tomb, your sins carried away. Say it out loud in the shop or the cab. Let the asking come second, after the Son has been named. You will find the asking changes once He is in front of it.

practices.title: GLORIFY GOD IN YOUR BODY
practices.body: You are not your own, Paul says, for you were bought with a price. If you belong to Christ, the Spirit lives in you, and your body is His house. Choose one ordinary thing you will do with your body this week for His sake — get to bed instead of scrolling, put the second drink back, go see your father. Do it because you were bought, not to buy anything. Your body is not a tool for earning God’s favor. It is a house He already paid for.

practices.title: REMEMBER WHAT HE SAID
practices.body: The disciples did not understand Destroy this temple until after He was raised. Then they remembered, and believed. Write John 2:19 on a card and carry it in your shirt pocket or your lunch pail this week. Each time you pull it out, read it slowly, as a man who already knows how the story ends. The temple was torn down. The temple was raised. Everything else hangs on that, and it is already done.

title: Zeal for His House
subtitle: from dust to the temple raised in three days
keyVerse: Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.

passage.text: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
He found in the temple those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and the changers of money sitting.
He made a whip of cords, and threw all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen; and he poured out the changers’ money and overthrew their tables.
To those who sold the doves, he said, “Take these things out of here! Don’t make my Father’s house a marketplace!”
His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will eat me up.”
The Jews therefore answered him, “What sign do you show us, seeing that you do these things?”
Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
The Jews therefore said, “It took forty-six years to build this temple! Will you raise it up in three days?”
But he spoke of the temple of his body.
When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he said this, and they believed the Scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.
Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs which he did.
But Jesus didn’t entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone,
and because he didn’t need for anyone to testify concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man.

stationsIntro: Take each verse slowly and let it land before you write. These five words come from the temple courts at Passover, and every one of them points to the Son who cleaned His Father’s house and then laid down His own body to be raised.
lifeIntro: This week is not about cleaning up your act before Sunday. Jesus has already cleared His Father’s house, laid down His body, and raised it again. These five practices are ways of living as a man whose body is now a house the Spirit lives in.
lifePulls: The temple in Jerusalem took forty-six years to build and would not stand forever. The temple of His body was torn down and raised, and it stands now at the right hand of the Father for you.
prayer: Father, thank You for sending Your Son into Your house with zeal for Your name. I confess the tables I have let into my own life and the coins I keep counting. I have treated You like a store and myself like a customer. Thank You that Jesus poured out the money and paid for me Himself. Thank You that His zeal carried Him to the cross, and that He went there for me. Thank You that the temple of His body was torn down and raised again. Turn over what does not belong in me, and make my body a house that honors You. Teach me to come to You as a son, and to remember His words when I do not yet understand them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, thank You for sending Your Son into Your house with zeal for Your name.
I confess the tables I have let into my own life and the coins I keep counting.
I have treated You like a store and myself like a customer.
Thank You that Jesus poured out the money and paid for me Himself.
Thank You that His zeal carried Him to the cross, and that He went there for me.
Thank You that the temple of His body was torn down and raised again.
Turn over what does not belong in me, and make my body a house that honors You.
Teach me to come to You as a son, and to remember His words when I do not yet understand them.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus walked into His Father’s house and found a market. He made a whip, poured out the coins, and turned over the tables. His zeal did not stop at the temple steps. It ate Him up at the cross. Then He told you plainly where God now meets men: in His body, torn down and raised. Stop trading with God. You were bought with a price you did not pay, and the temple stands.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see the tables on their sides. See the coins scattered across the stone, the small change of a thousand deals with God lying where it fell. See the Son of the house standing in the middle of it with a whip of cords in His hand, saying, My Father’s house. And see that He is not finished with what He started that Passover. He did not come to rearrange the market. He came to end it, and to give you a better house.

The dust told you to keep paying. It told you to keep your own ledger, slide your coins across the counter, and hope the account came out in your favor. But Jesus never came to run the store better. He came to close it. He let His zeal for His Father carry Him to the cross. He took the reproach that belonged to others. He received the vinegar, said It is finished, and gave up His spirit. The zeal that ate Him up was zeal for you, and it did not give out halfway.

Then the temple they tore down, He raised up. That body did not stay in the tomb. On the first day of the week the stone was taken away, and the risen Lord stood among His disciples and showed them his hands and his side. The wounds were still there. So was He — breathing on them, speaking to them, cooking them breakfast on the shore. That is the temple God meets you in now — not a building of forty-six years, but a Man who was dead and is alive, and who knows what is in you better than you do.

So walk into this week as a man who has been bought, not as a man still trying to pay. You do not have a bill outstanding. Nobody is coming to collect. The price is settled, and the Spirit has made a house of you. Christ knows every table you have let in, and He did not turn away. He said, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up — and He did. Lean your whole weight on the One who kept that word. The temple of His body is standing, and because it stands, you will stand too.
closingVerse: Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.
carry: Jesus cleared the market from His Father’s house and then named His own body, torn down and raised, as the temple; what trade are you still running with God that His raised body has already made needless?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men do not think they need to be born again. They think they need a tune-up. A little less temper. A little more time in the Word. Quit the second drink, call your father, get the money straight, and the engine will run. You may never say it that way, but you live it that way — as if your life with God were an old house you are bringing up to code one repair at a time, and the inspector will sign off once enough of the list is done.

Nicodemus is the best version of that man. He is learned, careful, respected and serious about God — the kind of man others call when they want a straight answer from the Scriptures. Nobody in John’s Gospel looks more finished. And the first thing Jesus tells him is that from where he stands he cannot even see the kingdom of God. Not because he has not tried hard enough. Trying was never the door. Nicodemus needs what you need — not more of himself, but a life he does not have and cannot make.

The dust says you are a decent man who needs adjusting. It will let you work on yourself for forty years, as long as you never admit you are dead. But a dead man does not need a better plan. He needs breath. The psalmist knew it. He did not ask God to help him improve; he asked God to give him life: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) John 3 is the night Jesus told a ruler the same thing — that what he needed was not repair but a birth, and that only God could give it.

sections.heading: A Man Who Came After Dark
pulls: Nicodemus came with a compliment and a question about signs. Jesus answered with a word about birth — because a man can admire every sign Jesus does and still be dead where it counts.
paras: The chapter break hides a seam. John 2 ends with many in Jerusalem believing because they saw His signs, and with Jesus refusing to trust Himself to them, for he himself knew what was in man. Then, without a pause, John writes Now there was a man. Nicodemus steps out of that crowd. He is one of the men whose heart Jesus has already read. He has seen what the crowd saw, and he wants to know more. That is a fair start, and Jesus will not let it be the finish.

He is a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews, and he appears three times in this Gospel. Here he comes in the dark with a compliment and a question. In John 7 he speaks up, carefully, for a fair hearing. At the end he comes with a hundred Roman pounds of myrrh and aloes for the body of Jesus. Read him across those pages and ask whether the wind of John 3:8 was moving in a man who could not have explained it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A RULER IN THE DARK
paras: Nicodemus opens with respect. Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him. Every word of that is true, and none of it is enough. He has watched the signs and drawn a sound conclusion. God is with this man. He is ready to file Jesus among the great teachers and talk shop.

Jesus will not be filed. He does not answer the compliment at all. Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom. Nicodemus came to discuss Jesus. Jesus turns the talk to Nicodemus — to the one thing about him that all his learning could not reach.

Mark the word see. Jesus does not say the unborn man cannot earn the kingdom or keep it. He says the man cannot see it. Nicodemus is sitting a few feet from the King, looking straight at Him, and does not know what he is looking at. That is the condition of every man before God gives him life. He is not a little short-sighted. He is blind. He can count the signs and miss the One they point to.

This is good news before it is hard news. If the trouble were effort, Jesus would have handed Nicodemus a list, and the man would have gone home and worked it — and you would be handed the same list. Instead Jesus names a birth. No one plans his own birth, earns it or sets the date. It is done to him, and it comes from outside him. That is exactly the help a dead man needs, and exactly the help God gives.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WATER AND SPIRIT
paras: Nicodemus hears the word birth and goes straight to the body. How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb, and be born? He is not being foolish. He is being plain about what he has to work with. A grown man cannot go back. He cannot unmake his years and start again from nothing. If the new birth is something a man must do, Nicodemus has just proved it impossible.

He is right, and Jesus lets him be right. Unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom. A teacher of Israel should have heard the echo. Through Ezekiel God had promised, I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean, and then, I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. Water to wash the filth away. Spirit to put life where stone had been. And every line is God speaking — I will, over and over, with no blank left for the man to fill in.

So this is no word about a rite a man arranges for himself. It is the promise of the prophets coming due: God washing a sinner and giving him a new heart by His own Spirit. Baptism is a sign of that washing, and the sign points away from itself to what God alone does.

Then Jesus draws the line. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. Flesh can be schooled, disciplined, dressed up and ordained, and it will still be flesh. It can only make more of itself. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Life of a new kind comes only from the One who gives life.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: WHERE THE WIND WANTS
pulls: You cannot order wind, store it, or shut it off. You only see what it does. The Spirit gives the new birth the same way — and a life that hangs on His will does not weaken in a bad week.
paras: Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born anew.’ The must is real. There is no side gate into the kingdom for decent men. But the must does not hand Nicodemus a job. Jesus explains it with the weather.

The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit. You cannot order wind. You cannot stand in the back field and tell it which way to come. You cannot store it in the barn or shut it off. You only see what it does — dust lifting off the road, the corn leaning, a shingle torn loose. The Spirit gives birth the same way. He moves where He pleases, and a man born of Him may not be able to say when or how. He only knows that he now loves what he once ignored, and that he trusts the One he once only admired.

That is a hard word for a man who likes control. It is also the only word that lets him rest. John said it at the front of his Gospel: those who believe were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. Your new life does not hang on your grip. It hangs on His will, and His will does not weaken in a bad week.

Nicodemus is still in the dark. How can these things be? Jesus presses him. Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things? The most learned man in the room is the man who needs to be born. Learning was never his lack. Life was.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: LOOK AND LIVE
paras: Now Jesus speaks as the one witness who has been where He is describing. No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man. Nicodemus has been trying to reason his way up. Jesus tells him the road runs one direction. No man climbs to God. God came down.

Then He reaches into the books Nicodemus knew best. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up. Go back to Numbers 21. Israel spoke against God and Moses, and Yahweh sent venomous snakes among the people, and they bit the people. Men were dying in the camp. They did not need a talk about snakes. They needed a cure, and God gave one strange enough that no man could take credit for it. Moses set a bronze serpent on a pole, and when he looked at the serpent of bronze, he lived.

Watch what the bitten man did. He did not cut out the poison. He did not prove he deserved to be healed. He looked — and the life came from what God had lifted up, not from the strength of his eyes. That is faith: a dying man’s gaze resting on the cure God provided.

The Son of Man must be lifted up the same way, on a pole of His own, so that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. Whoever. The man bitten worst looks at the same cross as the man bitten least. Nicodemus with all his learning and the drunk at the edge of the camp with none have one cure between them, and it is enough for both.

stations.verse: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.
stations.question: John brings in Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews, right after saying Jesus knew what was in man; what about my religious standing do I expect Jesus to be impressed by when He looks at me?
stations.live: Write down the one title or standing you lean on to feel right with God. Then pray over it plainly: ‘This gets me nothing in Your kingdom. Give me life.’
body: Archōn means a ruler or chief. The New Testament uses it for rulers of nations, for judges, and for members of the Sanhedrin — the sense here, where Nicodemus is a ruler of the Jews. John also uses it of the devil, the prince of this world, and Revelation uses it of Jesus Christ, the ruler of the kings of the earth.

Nicodemus had rank. He had a seat where decisions were made. None of it bought him an inch of the kingdom. Later John says that even many of the rulers believed in him, but would not confess it, so they would not be put out of the synagogue. Rank is heavy to carry into the light.

The dust says your standing counts — the crew you run, the name you built, the chair you hold at church. Archōn points past every ruler to the One who rules the kings of the earth, and He does not take a man in by rank. He takes him by birth.

stations.verse: The same came to him by night, and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.
stations.question: Nicodemus came by night and called Jesus a teacher come from God, true but far too small; where do I treat Jesus as a wise teacher to consult rather than the Lord who must give me life?
stations.live: Take the question you have been too ashamed or too unsure to bring to Jesus, and bring it tonight, after the house is quiet: ‘I don’t understand, but I am coming to You.’
body: Nyx is plain night. Here it stands in a form that marks when something happened: Nicodemus came by night. In John it is never only a clock. It carries a shadow. The night is coming, when no one can work, Jesus says. And when Judas walks out from the supper, John adds three words: It was night.

John never tells you why Nicodemus came after dark. He only keeps the detail. Near the end he names him again as the man who at first came to Jesus by night — and this time Nicodemus is carrying myrrh and aloes for the body of Jesus. The night was where he started. It was not where John left him.

The dust says Jesus only sees visitors in daylight, once your questions are sorted and your life is swept out. Nyx says He received a man in the dark, with nothing but a compliment and a muddle, and spoke to him words that still give life.

stations.verse: Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?
stations.question: Nicodemus asked, How can a man be born when he is old?, and he was right that no man can; where am I treating new life as a fresh start I must manage instead of a birth God gives?
stations.live: Name one thing you have written off as ‘just how I am’ after all these years. Bring it to God this week as a dead thing He can raise: ‘I can’t start over. You can make me new.’
body: Gerōn means an old man. This verse is the only place in the New Testament where it appears. In the Greek Old Testament it renders the Hebrew zaqen. Nicodemus reaches for it to say what he knows about himself: How can a man be born when he is old?

He may mean more than his age. A grown man is a settled thing. His habits have worn grooves. His temper has a history, and his regrets have names. He cannot go back to the start and come out different. Neither can you. Forty years of the same anger do not rinse out with a promise on Sunday night.

The dust says it is too late — that you are what the years have made you, and God is done shaping. But Jesus never asked Nicodemus to go back. He spoke of a birth that God gives. An old man cannot start over. God can make him new, at seventy as easily as at seven.

stations.verse: The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.
stations.question: Jesus likened everyone who is born of the Spirit to wind a man cannot see or steer, only hear; what change in my heart toward Christ can I point to that I know I did not make myself?
stations.live: Pick the man you have been trying to argue into the kingdom. This week stop pushing and pray for wind: ‘Lord, You blow where You want. Blow on him.’
body: Pneō means to breathe or to blow. It appears in seven New Testament verses, and in the Gospels it is the wind: the winds that blew and beat on the house built on the rock, the great wind blowing on the sea in the dark. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Psalm 147, where God causes his wind to blow, and the waters flow.

That is the picture Jesus hands Nicodemus. The wind blows where it wants to. No man commands it. You feel it on your face and see it bend the grass, but you did not start it and you cannot steer it. So it is with the new birth: real, felt, seen in what it does, and never at your command.

The dust wants a method — the right prayer, the right program, the right pressure on your son. Pneō answers that God blows where He wills, and He has blown on men harder and colder than the ones you are praying for.

stations.verse: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up.
stations.question: The bitten men in the camp were not told to treat their own wounds but to look at what God had lifted up; what sin am I still doctoring myself instead of looking to the Son of Man lifted up for it?
stations.live: When the old poison flares this week — the lust, the bitterness, the dread — do not start doctoring it yourself. Look to the cross first and say it: ‘He was lifted up for this. I look and live.’
body: Ophis is a serpent, a snake. In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly renders the Hebrew nachash. In the New Testament it can be a plain snake, a picture of cunning, or the devil himself, the old serpent. Paul uses it of the wilderness, where some perished by the serpents.

Here is the strange thing God did in Numbers 21. The cure for the bite looked like the thing that bit. Moses lifted a bronze serpent, and the dying looked at the shape of what was killing them. Jesus says He must be lifted up the same way. On the cross He bore the shape of your curse — made to be sin on our behalf — so that you could look and live.

The dust says the bite is your business: find the right treatment, manage the swelling, keep it covered. Ophis says the remedy has been lifted up where you can see it. You do not heal yourself. You look.

practices.title: COME AS YOU ARE, AFTER DARK
practices.body: Nicodemus came by night with questions he could not answer and a respect that fell short. Jesus received him. Set aside one late hour this week — after the house is asleep, or at the end of the night shift — and come to Jesus with what you actually have: doubt, confusion, a cold heart. Read John 3:1–15 aloud. Do not tidy your prayer first. He has already shown what He does with a man who comes in the dark.

practices.title: SET DOWN YOUR RANK
practices.body: Make a short list of what you have been counting on to stand right with God: years in church, a clean record, being the man who holds everything together. Lay it beside John 3:3. Then set it aside on purpose. Not one item on it can let you see the kingdom. Thank God that He gives new birth to men who bring nothing, because that is the only kind of man there has ever been.

practices.title: READ EZEKIEL 36
practices.body: Jesus expected a teacher of Israel to know where water and spirit came from. Read Ezekiel 36:25–27 slowly on three mornings this week. Count how many times God says I will.
