Then write one sentence about what He promises to wash away and one about what He promises to put in you. Let His promises, not your resolutions, tell you what the new birth is and who does the work of it.

practices.title: PRAY FOR WIND
practices.body: Name one man you love who has not yet been born anew — your brother, your son, the man who works the next bay over. You cannot argue him alive. Every morning this week, pray for him by name and ask the Spirit who blows where He wants to blow on him. Then do the plain things that are yours to do: tell him the truth, keep the door open, and wait without nagging.

practices.title: LOOK, AND KEEP LOOKING
practices.body: Faith is a bitten man looking at what God lifted up. When you fall this week, do not start by making repairs or proving you are sorry enough. Look first. Read John 3:14–15, name the sin plainly before God, and say: ‘The Son of Man was lifted up for this.’ Then get up and go back to work as a man who has eternal life, not a man still trying to earn it.

title: Born from Above
subtitle: from dust to a birth of the Spirit
keyVerse: Jesus answered him, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.

passage.text: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.
The same came to him by night, and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.”
Jesus answered him, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.”
Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?”
Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom.
That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born anew.’
The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”
Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?”
Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things?
Most certainly I tell you, we speak that which we know, and testify of that which we have seen, and you don’t receive our witness.
If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?
No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.
As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up,
that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE NEW BIRTH
stationsIntro: Five words from a conversation held in the dark. Read each verse slowly, let the question find you where you are, and let the Greek open what the English already says.
lifeIntro: God has done for you what you could never do for yourself. He sent His Son down from heaven, lifted Him up on a cross, and by His Spirit gives new birth to dead men. These five practices are ways of living like a man who has been born, not a man still trying to be. None of them is a ladder. Each one is a way of using the breath He has already given.
lifePulls: You cannot be born by trying harder, and you do not have to. The Spirit gives birth where He pleases, and the Son of Man was lifted up so that whoever looks to Him lives.
prayer: Father, I come to You the way Nicodemus came, with questions and nothing in my hands. I cannot make myself new. I cannot go back and start over, and I cannot climb up to You. Thank You that Your Son came down out of heaven for us. Thank You that He was lifted up, so that whoever believes in Him will not perish. Wash me with the clean water You promised, and put Your Spirit within me. Blow where You want in me, and in the men I love who are still in the dark. When the old poison bites, turn my eyes to the cross before I reach for my own cures. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I come to You the way Nicodemus came, with questions and nothing in my hands.
I cannot make myself new. I cannot go back and start over, and I cannot climb up to You.
Thank You that Your Son came down out of heaven for us.
Thank You that He was lifted up, so that whoever believes in Him will not perish.
Wash me with the clean water You promised, and put Your Spirit within me.
Blow where You want in me, and in the men I love who are still in the dark.
When the old poison bites, turn my eyes to the cross before I reach for my own cures.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Nicodemus had rank, learning and sincerity, and Jesus told him none of it would let him see God’s Kingdom. A man must be born anew, and no man gives birth to himself. God washes, God gives the new heart, God sends His Spirit like wind wherever He wants. Your part is the part of a bitten man in the camp: look at the Son of Man lifted up, and live.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, because everything you needed came down. You could not climb to God, so He descended out of heaven. You could not wash yourself, so He promised clean water. You could not give yourself a heart that beats for God, so He promised a new one, and His own Spirit to live in it. You could not cure the bite, so He let Himself be lifted up. Every step you could not take, He took toward you, and He did not stop short of the place where you were lying.

The dust told you that you were a decent man with a few repairs to make — or else a ruined man, too old to change. Both were lies. The decent man needed to be born. The ruined man can be. Jesus did not hand Nicodemus a ladder that night. He told him about the wind, and the wind does not ask how old a man is or how long he has lain in the dirt. It does not wait for him to be ready. It comes, and the dead man finds he is breathing, and the first thing he does with his new breath is call on the name of the Son.

So look where Moses told Israel to look. At the middle of a dying camp a pole stood up against the sky, and every bitten man who turned his eyes to it lived. Your pole is a cross outside Jerusalem. On it hung the Son of Man, made to be sin for you, carrying the shape of your curse so that it would not stay on you. He was lifted up there, and then He was lifted again — out of the grave, alive, never to die again, holding the life He now gives away.

Carry this into Tuesday. When the old poison rises, you do not have to treat it before you are allowed to look. Look first. The promise of John 3:15 is not that whoever tries hard enough will be spared, but that whoever believes in Him will not perish and will have eternal life — and that life begins now, at the tool bench, on the porch, in the hospital waiting room. The wind has blown. The serpent has been lifted. Look, and live.
closingVerse: Jesus answered him, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.
carry: Jesus told a respected teacher, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom; what are you still offering God from your own record, when what you need is the life only His Spirit gives?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: You have known John 3:16 longer than almost anything else in the Bible. You may have said it before you could read it. You have heard it at funerals and seen it painted on signs, and that is the danger. A verse that familiar stops being read. It turns into a sound, like the hum of the refrigerator — always running, never heard. You could finish it in your sleep, and that is not the same as having heard it.

And the dust has its own reading ready. It tells you God’s love is a mood — warm when you are doing well, cooling when you are not. Or it tells you the opposite lie: that God loves so loosely He cannot be angry about anything, so sin is a small matter and judgment is a word for other men. Either way the love shrinks. In the first lie it shrinks to the size of your performance. In the second it shrinks to a shrug.

John 3 will not sit still for either one. It measures God’s love by a gift, not a feeling. And it sets that love in the same chapter as the plainest word about God’s wrath anywhere in this Gospel. You need both, because a man face down in the dirt needs more than kind words. He needs a rescue that cost something, and he needs to know what God did with the anger his sin deserved. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Here is the word that revives. Read it this week as if the ink were still wet.

sections.heading: The End of the Night, and a Last Witness
pulls: John 3:16 does not tell you how warm God felt. It tells you what He gave. The love is measured by the gift, and the gift was His one and only Son lifted up on a cross.
paras: These verses run straight on from the night talk with Nicodemus. The For that opens 3:16 hooks it to what Jesus has just said about Moses and the bronze serpent. Do not pry the verse loose from that pole. The love of God in John 3 has a shape, and the shape is the Son of Man lifted up. The God who loves the world is the God who told Moses to raise that pole in a dying camp. Love here is not a warm feeling drifting over the camp. It is a cure set up in the middle of it.

Then the scene moves out to the Judean countryside, where Jesus is staying with His disciples and they are baptizing, while John the Baptist is still at work at Enon. John’s disciples are troubled that everyone is going to Jesus. Their teacher has pointed at Jesus since the first chapter, and here he does it one last time. John’s answer is his last testimony in this Gospel, and the chapter closes where it has to close: life for the one who believes the Son, and wrath that remains on the one who will not.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: GOD SO LOVED
paras: Read it slowly. For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son. The verse does not say God felt deeply. It says He gave. You learn the size of a man’s love by what it costs him — the double shifts he works so his kids can eat, the night he sits up with a feverish child, the kidney he gives his brother. You learn the size of God’s love the same way. He gave the Son who is in the bosom of the Father. There was nothing larger to give.

And He gave Him to the world. Do not make that word soft. In this Gospel the world is the place that didn’t recognize him, the place that hates Him because He tells it its works are evil. God did not love a world that was lovable. He loved a world in rebellion, and you were standing in it with your fists up.

Then comes the widest door in Scripture. Whoever believes in him. Not whoever was raised right, not whoever has cleaned up, not whoever was born on the right side of the river. Whoever. The offer is free and it is real, and it is made to every man who hears it, including you. No one who comes to the Son is turned away.

What does the believer receive? First, he should not perish. Perish is a hard word. It is the end of a man left under the judgment of God, and it stands in the verse to tell you what you are being saved from. And in its place, eternal life — not a prize held back at the end of a long probation, but life the believer has now, because he has the Son.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: NOT SENT TO JUDGE
paras: For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him. Most men assume that if God came close it would be to settle accounts. That is what you would do with a hired man who had robbed you blind. But the Son did not come down carrying a ledger. He came carrying a rescue.

That does not make judgment a fiction. He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already. Read the second line again. The unbeliever is not waiting for a verdict. He is already under one. Christ walked into a courtroom where the sentence had already been read, and He came to save.

Why, then, do men stay under it? The light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light; for their works were evil. The trouble is love — the wrong love. Everyone who does evil hates the light, and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed. You know this in your own bones: the history you clear, the receipt you hide, the answer you shade when your wife asks where you were. Darkness feels safer because nobody sees. No man hides a thing in the dark that he is proud of.

But the light of Christ does not expose a man to shame him. It exposes him to heal him. He who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God. The man who steps into the light finds that even his stepping was God’s work in him. The light he feared was the only place he could be washed.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE FRIEND OF THE BRIDEGROOM
pulls: John the Baptist watched the crowds leave him for Jesus and called it full joy. A man is set free the day he stops needing to be the center — because Christ already is, and always was.
paras: The scene changes. Jesus is in the Judean countryside with His disciples, and John the Baptist is still baptizing at Enon, because there was much water there. A dispute starts, and John’s disciples carry the news to him like men reporting on a rival outfit: he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him. They expect their teacher to be stung. A crowd is a preacher’s harvest, and John’s is thinning. Men have split churches over less.

John answers with a sentence that would end most quarrels in most churches. A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven. Whatever John had, God gave him. Whatever Jesus has, God gave Him. There is nothing to guard.

Then he reaches for a wedding. He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. John is not the groom. The bride is not his. His work was to stand near, to hear the groom’s voice, and to be glad. A friend who wanted the bride for himself would be a traitor at that wedding. The friend who brings her to the groom and steps back has done his work well. This, my joy, therefore is made full.

Then comes the line every servant of Christ has to learn. He must increase, but I must decrease. John does not say it through his teeth. He says it as a man whose joy is full. There is a freedom in being second. You do not have to be the center of your family, your church or your work. Christ already is, and He carries the weight of it far better than you ever could.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE WRATH THAT REMAINS
paras: The chapter closes by lifting Jesus above every other voice. He who comes from above is above all. John speaks as a man of the earth. Jesus speaks from heaven, and God gives the Spirit without measure. Then this: The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. Everything — your life, your judgment, your future — rests in that hand.

So the last verse is a fork in the road with no third path. One who believes in the Son has eternal life. Has — held now, not hoped for later. But one who disobeys the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. Do not sand that down. God’s wrath is not a temper He loses. It is His settled, holy opposition to sin, and it already rests on the man who refuses the Son. It remains. It does not fade with time or wear off under good behavior.

That is the hardest sentence in the chapter, and it is why the rest of the chapter is such good news. The wrath does not have to remain. There is one place it has already fallen in full: on the Son lifted up. Paul says it plainly: being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him. And 1 John 4:10 says God sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. The storm broke on Christ so that it would not break on you.

That is what it means that God so loved the world. He did not wave His wrath away. He bore it Himself in His Son, and He offers shelter to every man who will come under it. Believe the Son, and the verdict over you is life.

stations.verse: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
stations.question: John says God so loved the world, the same world that didn’t recognize him and loved the darkness; how does it change the way I come to God this week that He loved me while I stood against Him?
stations.gloss: order; the world; the world of men
stations.live: Write John 3:16 on a card, and wherever it says the world, write your own name beside it. Carry the card this week. You were not loved for standing out from the world. You were loved in it.
body: Kosmos first meant order, then an ornament — Peter uses it for outward adorning. From there it came to mean the ordered universe, then the earth, then the people who live on it. In its sharpest sense it names mankind set against God, the world that hates me, Jesus says, because I testify about it, that its works are evil.

It runs all through this Gospel. Of the 150 New Testament verses where it appears, 57 are in John’s Gospel, and seventeen more in 1 John. And in 3:16 it carries its whole weight at once: the world God made, the people in it, and their rebellion against Him. That is the world He loved.

The dust says God’s love goes to men who have something to recommend them. Kosmos says He loved the ones who did not recognize Him and would not have Him — and you were among them when He gave His Son. He did not wait for the world to turn around first.

stations.verse: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
stations.question: Jesus said whoever believes in the Son should not perish, but have eternal life; what would change in how I face this week’s trouble if I believed that life is already mine in Him?
stations.live: Each morning this week, before you pick up your phone, say John 3:36 aloud: ‘One who believes in the Son has eternal life.’ Lean on the word has, and go to work as a man who holds it.
body: Aiōnios is built on aiōn and means age-long, eternal. It can describe what has neither beginning nor end, like the eternal Spirit; what has no beginning, like the grace God gave in Christ before time began; or what has no end, like the blood of an eternal covenant. Very often it stands beside the word for life.

John’s Gospel has it in seventeen verses, nearly always as eternal life. And in John, eternal life is not only long. It has a Person in it. This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ. It begins the day a man believes.
The dust says eternal life is a prize at the far end, held back until you prove you deserve it. Jesus says the believer has it — life that will not run out, held in a hand no one can pry open.

stations.verse: He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.
stations.question: When his disciples complained that everyone is coming to him, John said the bridegroom’s friend rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice; where do I resent Christ getting attention I wanted for myself?
stations.live: Do one piece of real work for someone this week and make sure you get no credit for it. When the itch for notice comes, answer it: ‘He is the Bridegroom. I am glad to be His friend.’
body: Nymphios is a bridegroom. It appears in twelve New Testament verses: in Jesus’ word about the friends of the bridegroom, who cannot mourn while he is with them; in the parable of the ten virgins; and at Cana, where the bridegroom was praised for good wine he never supplied.

John the Baptist knew which man at the wedding he was. Not the groom — the friend who stands near, hears the groom’s voice, and is glad. The bride belongs to Christ. Every man who serves her, from the pulpit or from the head of his own table, is a friend of the groom and never the groom.
The dust wants you at the center of the wedding pictures. Nymphios says the joy is in hearing the Bridegroom’s voice — and He has already claimed His bride, you among her, and He will keep her.

stations.verse: He must increase, but I must decrease.
stations.question: John said He must increase, but I must decrease as a man whose joy was made full; where this week am I straining to stay at the center of a place that Christ already holds?
stations.gloss: to make less; to be made lower
stations.live: In one conversation this week where you would normally make sure your point lands, let it go and point to Christ instead. Afterward say it plainly: ‘He must increase. I must decrease.’
body: Elattoō means to make less. It stands in only three New Testament verses. Here it is passive: I must decrease. The other two are in Hebrews 2. The first quotes Psalm 8; the second applies it to Jesus, made a little lower than the angels.

That changes how John’s sentence sounds. Before John ever said I must decrease, the Son of God had already been made less — taking flesh, taking the low place, that by the grace of God he should taste of death for everyone. John is following the Lord who went lower first, and went lower for him. There is no shame on a road the Son of God has already walked.
The dust says that to be less is to lose. Elattoō says the Son of God was made lower for you and then crowned with glory and honor. The man who decreases under Him loses nothing he will miss.

stations.verse: One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.
stations.question: Since the wrath of God remains on the man who refuses the Son, where am I treating my sin as something time or good behavior will wear off, instead of bringing it under the Son who bore that wrath?
stations.live: Read Romans 5:9 and John 3:36 side by side each night this week. Then thank God out loud: ‘The wrath that should remain on me fell on Your Son. I am under His blood.’
body: Orgē is anger, wrath. It is used of men’s anger, which Paul tells you to put away. Used of God, it names the reaction of His nature against sin, and also what that reaction brings down on the sinner. This verse is the only place in John’s Gospel where the word appears.

Look at the verb beside it: the wrath remains. The man who refuses the Son is not drifting toward a judgment that may never come. He is under it now, and it stays. That is the plain truth about every man outside Christ — and it was the truth about you before God gave you faith.

The dust says God’s wrath is either a myth or a weight you must carry alone. Orgē meets the gospel at the cross: being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him. The wrath fell. It fell on Christ.

practices.title: ONE PHRASE A DAY
practices.body: Take John 3:16 one phrase a day: For God so loved the world; he gave his one and only Son; whoever believes in him; should not perish; eternal life. Write each phrase at the top of a page, and under it write one plain sentence about what it means for you this week. Let the old verse become strange enough to hear again, and thank God for each phrase by name. Do not hurry to the end of the verse; the week is long enough for all of it.

practices.title: COME INTO THE LIGHT
practices.body: Name the one thing you keep in the dark — the account she does not know about, the late-night screen, the lie you told your boss and kept telling. Jesus says the man who does evil stays away lest his works would be exposed. But the light of Christ exposes to heal. Confess it to God this week, then to one trusted brother who will pray with you. Walk into the light on purpose. Nothing you bring into His light is news to Him.

practices.title: TAKE SECOND PLACE GLADLY
practices.body: John the Baptist watched his crowd walk away to Jesus and called his joy full. Pick one place this week where you usually need to be seen — the crew meeting, the family argument, the Sunday school class. Make Christ the subject and yourself the friend who stands near. Keep quiet about your part. Then notice the strange relief of not having to be the center. Christ does not need your help to be seen, and neither do you.

practices.title: PUT IT IN HIS HAND
practices.body: The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. Name the three things you are gripping hardest right now — a son, a debt, a diagnosis, a job. Each night this week, name them to the Father one at a time and say: ‘This is already in the Son’s hand.’ Then open your own hands, palms up, and leave them open. You were never built to hold the world.

practices.title: INVITE ONE MAN UNDER THE SHELTER
practices.body: God so loved the world, and the world is made of names. Choose one man who does not believe — a neighbor down the road, a man on the night shift, your own brother. Pray for him by name each day. When the opening comes, do not hide the hard half to keep the easy half pleasant. Tell him the wrath is real and the Son still receives every man who comes. Mercy only sounds like good news when the danger is real, and the danger is real.

title: God So Loved the World
subtitle: from dust to eternal life
keyVerse: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

passage.text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God.
This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light; for their works were evil.
For everyone who does evil hates the light, and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed.
But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”
After these things, Jesus came with his disciples into the land of Judea. He stayed there with them and baptized.
John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there. They came, and were baptized;
for John was not yet thrown into prison.
Therefore a dispute arose on the part of John’s disciples with some Jews about purification.
They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.”
John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.
You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all.
What he has seen and heard, of that he testifies; and no one receives his witness.
He who has received his witness has set his seal to this, that God is true.
For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God gives the Spirit without measure.
The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.
One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.”

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE LOVE OF GOD
stationsIntro: These five words carry the best-known verse in the Bible and the hardest verse in its chapter. Read slowly, as if for the first time, and let each word sharpen what you thought you already knew.
lifeIntro: God loved a world set against Him, and He proved it with a gift: His Son, lifted up, bearing the wrath that would have remained on you. Whoever believes in Him has life now. These practices are a believer’s way of living inside that love for the next seven days. Nothing in them earns that love. Every one of them starts from it.
lifePulls: God did not wave His wrath away, and He did not leave you under it. He gave His one and only Son to bear it — and whoever believes in Him has eternal life today.
prayer: Father, You so loved the world that You gave Your one and only Son. You loved me while I stood in that world with my back to You. Thank You that Your Son did not come to judge me but to save me. Thank You that the wrath I earned fell on Him, and that I have eternal life in His name. Bring what I hide into Your light, and let Your light wash me. Make me glad to decrease, so that Christ increases in my house and in my work. I put into the Son’s hand what I cannot hold. Give me courage to tell one man this week where the wrath went. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You so loved the world that You gave Your one and only Son.
You loved me while I stood in that world with my back to You.
Thank You that Your Son did not come to judge me but to save me.
Thank You that the wrath I earned fell on Him, and that I have eternal life in His name.
Bring what I hide into Your light, and let Your light wash me.
Make me glad to decrease, so that Christ increases in my house and in my work.
I put into the Son’s hand what I cannot hold.
Give me courage to tell one man this week where the wrath went.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: God’s love is not a mood. It is measured by a gift: His one and only Son, lifted up for a world that hated Him. Whoever believes in Him is not judged and has eternal life now. Whoever refuses Him stays under the wrath of God, and it does not wear off. There is one way out from under it. Believe the Son, come into the light, and let Him increase.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and read the old verse again as if the ink were still wet. God so loved — not the version of you that shows up on a good Sunday, but a world that did not know Him. God so loved — not with a sigh from a safe distance, but with a gift that cost Him His Son. God so loved — and the love did not stop at feeling. It went all the way to a cross, where the Son of Man was lifted up like the bronze serpent so that dying men could look and live.

The dust told you that God’s love rises and falls with your week, or that His love is so soft His wrath cannot be real. Both lies make Him smaller. John 3 makes Him larger in both directions. His wrath against sin is real, and it remains on every man who refuses the Son. His love is larger still, because it went under that wrath on purpose to bring you out from under it. You do not have to choose between a God who is holy and a God who is kind. At the cross you meet both, and neither is watered down.

So see where the wrath went. It did not drift off, and it was not excused. It fell on Christ. The Father loved the Son, and still He gave Him. The Son loved the Father, and still He drank the cup the Father handed Him. He bore what you had earned until He could say It is finished and give up His spirit. Then the grave gave Him back. The One who had been lifted up on the cross walked out alive, and the eternal life He gives you is His own risen life.

When the wrath you deserve feels close this week and the love you have heard about feels far, go back to the verb. Jesus did not say that whoever believes might someday have life. He said the one who believes in the Son has eternal life. Has it today — at the work bench, at the supper table, in the sleepless hour before dawn. The wrath that should have remained on you fell on Him, and it will not come back for a second payment. You stand under His shelter with eternal life already in your hands.
closingVerse: For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
carry: Since God measured His love for you by the gift of his one and only Son, where this week will you stop reading His love off your circumstances and read it off the cross?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man has a well he keeps walking back to. For one it is the phone after the house goes quiet. For another it is the second drink, or the paycheck he counts twice and still finds short. For another it is the nod from the men at the feed store, the sense that people think he is good at what he does. You go, you draw, you drink, and for an hour the ache backs off. Then you are dry again, and you reach for the rope.

The dust has a story about that. It says the thirst is the problem, and the fix is more water from the same hole. Dig deeper. Work longer. Find a better woman, a bigger job, a quieter house. It never says the well is the problem. It never tells you that you were made to drink from something that does not run out, and that every bucket you lower is a quiet admission you have not found it yet.

And when the dust cannot sell you more water, it sells you shame instead. It tells you that a man with your record, who has drawn from the wells you have drawn from, would not be welcome at a clean spring. So you stay at the old hole and keep pulling up mud. A man who has given up on water ends up face down where the psalmist lay: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)
John 4 meets that man at the bottom of his rope. Jesus sits down at a well, tired, and asks a woman with a ruined name for a drink — so that He can give her water she will never have to draw again.

sections.heading: A Tired Man at Jacob’s Well
pulls: The dust says your thirst means you need more of the same water. Jesus sits down at your well and says the thirst means you were made for a spring — and He is the One who gives it.
paras: John has just told you that God so loved the world. Now he shows you what that love does on foot. Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee, and John says He needed to pass through Samaria. The need was not in the road. It was in the will of the Father who sent Him, because the Father was seeking a worshiper in Sychar. He comes near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son, Joseph, and sits down. Jesus therefore, being tired — the Word who made the world is worn out from walking it.

Read John 4:1–26 straight through before you go further. Watch how the talk moves. It starts with a cup of water and ends with I am he, the one who speaks to you. In between, Jesus offers a gift, uncovers a life, and opens the door of worship to a woman who thought every door had been shut on her. Each step is His. She does not climb toward Him. He comes down to her and keeps coming.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: GIVE ME A DRINK
paras: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. She comes with her jar and her rope, the way she has come more times than she could count. The first thing the Son of God says to her is a request: Give me a drink. The One who will give living water begins by asking for well water. He makes Himself the one in need.

She hears it as a rule broken in broad daylight. How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman? John adds the reason she is startled: Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. A wall stood between their peoples. His own disciples will soon show you another one, when they come back and marvel that He is talking with a woman at all. And she carries a third wall of her own, which He is about to name. Jesus steps over every one of them for a cup of water.

Then He turns the talk. If you knew the gift of God, He says, and who it is that is asking, you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water. She lacks two things — the gift and the Giver — and between them they are the whole gospel. Salvation is a gift, not a wage. And the gift cannot be pried loose from the Man who gives it.

Notice the order. Ask, and He gives. No labor is put in front of the gift. No bucket, no rope, no climb down into the dark. Living water is spring water, running and fresh, the kind God called Himself through Jeremiah: the spring of living waters. The thirsty woman thinks she is doing a stranger a favor. In fact the stranger is offering her God.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A SPRING INSIDE YOU
paras: She looks at His empty hands. Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. She is right about the well and wrong about the Man. Are you greater than our father, Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself? The answer is yes, and John wrote his whole book to say so.

Jesus does not argue about Jacob. He points at the water. Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again. That is the plain truth about every well you own. The raise satisfies until the bills catch up with it. The praise lasts until the next job. The bottle and the screen are worse, because they leave you thirstier than they found you. You are not strange for being thirsty again. You were made for something those wells cannot hold, and no amount of rope will change that.

Then comes the promise: whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again. And more than that: the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life. He does not hand you a jar to carry home and ration through the week. He puts the spring inside you. Later John tells you plainly what the water is: he said this about the Spirit. It is the life of God Himself, given to live in a man, rising and not running down.

She answers like a worn-out worker: Sir, give me this water, so that I don’t get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw. She still thinks in buckets. But she has asked. And He will not leave her there.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: GO, CALL YOUR HUSBAND
pulls: Jesus names the sin plainly and stays at the well. He tells the whole truth about a man and does not walk away from him, because He came there to give water, not to condemn.
paras: Go, call your husband, and come here. Why does Jesus turn to the hardest thing in her life? Not to shame her. Living water is not poured into a woman who insists she is not thirsty, and her thirst had a history.

I have no husband, she says. It is true as far as it goes. Jesus finishes the sentence for her: you have had five husbands; and he whom you now have is not your husband. John does not tell you how each marriage ended, and you should not guess. He tells you what Jesus said. Five, and now a man who is not hers. Her life had been a row of wells. Each one promised water, each one ran dry, and the last one she had not even called a marriage.

Watch what Jesus does not do. He does not lecture. He does not get up and leave. He names the sin plainly and stays at the well. You said well — He even credits her with the true part of what she said. That is how the Son of God handles a sinner He has come to save. He tells the whole truth, and He stays.

Before you look down on her, look at your own wells. The silence toward your wife. The money you keep where she will not see it. The grudge you water every night. Jesus knows your list the way He knew hers, every line of it, and He has not walked off from you either. Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet, she says. She sees that He knows. What she does not see yet is that He knows everything and is still offering the water.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE FATHER SEEKS
paras: She reaches for an argument about mountains. Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, and you Jews say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship. Men do this when the talk gets close to the bone. Jesus lets her change the subject, then turns it back to the center. The hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. Not this mountain or that city. Worship is moving to a Person — to the Man sitting on the edge of Jacob’s well, whose body John has already called the temple.

Then comes the line that turns the chapter: for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers. You thought she came looking for water. You thought you came looking for God. The Father was looking first. He sent His Son through Samaria, sat Him down at the sixth hour, and had Him wait for a woman everyone else had stopped waiting for. That is how a dry soul becomes a worshiper. God goes after him.

God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. That word must is not a ladder for you to climb. The Spirit is the water Jesus gives, and the truth is standing in front of her. What God requires, God supplies.

She reaches for her last hope: I know that Messiah comes, he who is called Christ. Jesus does not make her wait. I am he, the one who speaks to you. The Messiah she was hoping for someday was sitting in the dust beside her, thirsty, and He had come for her. He has come down the same road for you, and He is speaking to you now. Drink.

stations.verse: The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
stations.question: The woman was startled that a Jew would ask her for a drink, since Jews have no dealings with Samaritans; which man have I left on the far side of a line Jesus Himself crossed on purpose?
stations.gloss: to use together with; to have dealings with
stations.live: Name one man you have treated as beyond dealings — because of his people, his past, or what he did to you. This week, share something ordinary with him: a cup of coffee, a ride, a hand on a job.
body: Synchraomai appears only here in the New Testament. At bottom it means to use something together with someone; with people in view, it comes to mean to associate with, to have dealings with. John uses it to explain her shock: Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.

Lay that plain sense beside the scene. Jesus asks for a drink from her hand, out of her jar, on her rope. The very thing the word says Jews and Samaritans did not do, He does first, and He does it on purpose. He shares what is hers before He offers what is His. A man who has spent years believing that clean people keep their distance from him needs to watch Jesus reach for that jar.
The dust wants you to believe there is a line you crossed that God will not cross back. Synchraomai names the line, and Jesus walks across it with His hand out.

stations.verse: The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. So where do you get that living water?
stations.question: She looked at His empty hands and said, Sir, you have nothing to draw with; where am I sizing up what Jesus can do for me by what I can see in His hands instead of by who He is?
stations.gloss: a vessel to draw with; a bucket
stations.live: When you pray this week, bring no record of what you have done. Open your hands at the start and say it plainly: ‘I have nothing to draw with. You give.’
body: Antlēma properly means what is drawn, and then the vessel you draw it with — a bucket. The New Testament has no other instance of it; John 4:11 is the lone use.

Her objection is sound as far as it goes. Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. She measures Jesus by His gear and finds Him short. She cannot yet see that He does not draw living water from anywhere. He is its spring. Men do the same with God. They look for the gear: the program, the effort, the rope a man has to braid for himself before heaven will pay attention.

The dust says no bucket, no water, so get to work and make one. The gospel answers that the gift needs no bucket of yours. Jesus said you would have asked him, and he would have given. The asking is the only tool required, and even the asking is His gift.

stations.verse: The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. So where do you get that living water?
stations.question: Jacob’s well was the best water she knew, and the well is deep, yet Jesus says everyone who drinks it will thirst again; what well do I keep going back to that has never once kept me from thirsting again?
stations.gloss: a well; a shaft sunk deep into the ground
stations.live: Name your deepest well — the one you go back to when no one is watching. Tell one trusted man this week where it is, and ask him to ask you about it on Friday.
body: Phrear is a well, and the Greek Old Testament uses it chiefly for the Hebrew be’er. Five New Testament verses carry it. Two name Jacob’s well in this conversation, and two in Revelation name the pit of the abyss.

That range tells the truth. A well can give water, and a well can swallow a man. Jesus once asked the Pharisees which of them would not pull out a son or an ox that fell into a well on the Sabbath. The wells you dig for yourself run deep, and more than one man has fallen into his own and could not climb out.

The dust says dig deeper and you will strike the water that lasts. But the well is deep and the water down there is the same water. Christ did not come to lower you further down the shaft. He came down to where you had fallen, to lift you out.

stations.verse: But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.
stations.question: Jesus promises her no fuller jar but water that will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life; where am I living as if my life with God depends on my refilling it instead of on His spring?
stations.gloss: to leap; of water, to spring up
stations.live: On the morning you feel driest this week, do not try to work up a feeling. Read John 4:14 out loud and say: ‘This spring is His, and it is still rising.’
body: Hallomai means to leap. Luke uses it twice in Acts for lame men made whole — Leaping up, he stood and began to walk — and John uses it once, here, of water springing up. Three verses in the whole New Testament, and in each it is life on the move where there had been none.

Jesus says His water will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life. Not a jar on the shelf. Not a tank you drain by Friday. A spring, leaping up from inside, fed from a source you cannot see and did not dig. The life He gives does not depend on your pumping. It depends on Him.

The dust tells you your faith is running low and you had better ration what is left. Hallomai answers that what Christ put in you leaps. It rose on Monday, and it will rise again on Tuesday, because He is the One who keeps it rising.

stations.verse: But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.
stations.question: When the talk came close, the woman turned it to which mountain was right, and Jesus answered that the Father seeks such to be his worshipers; where have I hidden behind arguments about religion while the Father was seeking me?
stations.live: Before work one morning this week, give God five minutes of worship with no requests in it. Begin it this way: ‘Father, You came looking for me first.’
body: Proskynētēs is a worshiper, a noun made from the common verb for worship. In English the word worship runs again and again through these five verses, but this noun stands alone: one verse in the New Testament, and Jesus is the one who says it.

He spends that one use on a sentence about the Father’s desire: the Father seeks such to be his worshipers. Worshipers are not volunteers God puts up with. They are people He goes after. He went after a Samaritan woman at a well in the middle of a working day, and He went after her through His own Son, tired and thirsty and sitting in the dust.

The dust says worship is for clean men on good weeks, and you can come back once you have sorted yourself out. The Father does not wait for that. He seeks. The one time the New Testament uses this word, a seeking Father stands behind it.

practices.title: NAME YOUR WELLS
practices.body: Jesus said Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again. Take a sheet of paper and write down the wells you keep going back to: the screen, the bottle, the overtime, the good opinion of other men, the account balance you check three times a day. Be specific. Under them all, write one line: None of these has ever made me stop being thirsty. You are not being condemned by the list. You are being shown where the water is not.

practices.title: ASK BEFORE YOU WORK
practices.body: You would have asked him, and he would have given you living water. The order is ask, then receive. Each morning this week, before you pick up the phone or turn the key, ask Christ in plain words for what He promised: ‘Give me this water.’ Do not bargain. Do not list what you will do for Him in return. A thirsty man asks, and the Giver keeps His word. Let that be the first thing you do every day.

practices.title: LET HIM NAME IT
practices.body: Jesus named the woman’s sin and stayed at the well. Sit down once this week and let Him do the same with you. Read John 4:16–18, then tell Him the plain truth about the thing you call by a softer name — the grudge, the hidden account, the way you talk to your wife when you are tired. Say it out loud before Him. Then read John 4:14 again. He tells the truth, and He does not get up and leave.

practices.title: CROSS ONE LINE
practices.body: Jesus asked for a drink from a woman His people had no dealings with. Think of the man you have filed under no dealings — the neighbor on the other side of the fence, the brother you cut off, the worker you look past every day. This week, cross the line with something ordinary: a cup of coffee, a hand loading the trailer, a phone call. Christ reached across a wall to get to you. Now reach across one.

practices.title: WORSHIP AS ONE SOUGHT
practices.body: The Father seeks such to be his worshipers. On the Lord’s Day, walk into worship as a man who was looked for, not a man who has to earn his seat. Before the service begins, read John 4:23 and say it back: ‘He sought me.’ Sing the songs as answers to a God who came to your well first. Pray the prayers as a man already found. Then go home and drink, and let what He gives rise in you all week.

title: Living Water
subtitle: from dust to a spring that never runs dry
keyVerse: But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.

passage.text: Therefore when the Lord knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John
(although Jesus himself didn’t baptize, but his disciples),
he left Judea and departed into Galilee.
He needed to pass through Samaria.
So he came to a city of Samaria, called Sychar, near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son, Joseph.
Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being tired from his journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour.
A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”
For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.
The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. So where do you get that living water?
Are you greater than our father, Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his children and his livestock?”
Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,
but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I don’t get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw.”
Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”
The woman answered, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You said well, ‘I have no husband,’
for you have had five husbands; and he whom you now have is not your husband. This you have said truly.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.
Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, and you Jews say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”
Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour comes, when neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, will you worship the Father.
You worship that which you don’t know. We worship that which we know; for salvation is from the Jews.
But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”
The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah comes, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things.”
Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”

stationsIntro: Jacob’s well holds the vocabulary of grace this week: a broken rule, a bucket, a shaft, a spring, a worshiper. Take each verse as it comes, give the question a straight answer, and watch each word open up the gift Jesus is holding out.
lifeIntro: Jesus crossed every wall to sit at that well, and He has crossed them to reach you. He gives the water as a gift and keeps it springing up. A thirsty man drinks by asking, and these five practices are ways of asking.
lifePulls: Every well this world digs leaves you thirsty again. The water Jesus gives does not sit in a jar you have to guard. It rises in you, because He put it there and He keeps it rising.
prayer: Father, You sent Your Son through Samaria for a woman no one else was waiting for, and You sent Him for me. Lord Jesus, You sat tired by the well. You know what it is to be worn out and thirsty. I confess the wells I keep walking back to, though they have never once satisfied me. You know everything I have done, and You have not walked away. Give me the water You promised, the water that becomes a spring and does not run dry. Holy Spirit, rise up in me on the mornings I feel driest. Make me a worshiper in spirit and truth, because You sought me first. When the old wells call to me this week, turn my eyes back to the spring You have opened in me. Help me cross the line toward the man I have written off, the way You crossed it toward me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You sent Your Son through Samaria for a woman no one else was
waiting for, and You sent Him for me.
Lord Jesus, You sat tired by the well. You know what it is to be worn out and thirsty.
I confess the wells I keep walking back to, though they have never once satisfied me.
You know everything I have done, and You have not walked away.
Give me the water You promised, the water that becomes a spring and does not run dry.
Holy Spirit, rise up in me on the mornings I feel driest.
Make me a worshiper in spirit and truth, because You sought me first.
When the old wells call to me this week, turn my eyes back to the spring You have opened in me.
Help me cross the line toward the man I have written off, the way You crossed it toward me.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Jesus needed to pass through Samaria because the Father was seeking a worshiper there. He asked a woman for water so He could give her His own. He named her five husbands plainly and did not walk away. Every well you dig will leave you thirsty again. Stop lowering the rope. Ask Him, and He gives water that becomes a spring inside you, rising to eternal life.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, from the rope in your hands. You have been drawing from the same deep hole for years. You drew when you were lonely. You drew when you were proud. You drew when the house went quiet and the night got long. You drew when the money was good, and you drew harder when it was gone. And every time, the water ran out before the morning did.

Now look who is sitting on the edge of your well. Not a stranger with a sermon. The Son of God, tired from the road, asking for a drink. He came the long way to be here. He knows everything you have done — every name on your list, every bucket you lowered in the dark — and He has not stood up to leave. He did not come to this well to drink. He came to give, and He came to give to you. He asked her for water so that she would ask Him for His, and He is asking the same of you.

And He paid for the giving. The One who promised that whoever drinks His water will never thirst again hung on a cross at the end and said I am thirsty. He took the dryness of your sin into His own mouth. He went down into the place where there is no water at all, so that a spring could be opened in you. The thirst you had coming, He drank. The water He alone deserved, He hands to you as a gift.

So drink, and keep drinking. Not because you have earned the cup, but because He offered it, and He does not take His gifts back. When the old wells call you on Tuesday, they will still be deep and still be dry. But there is a spring in you now that you did not dig. It rose this morning. It will rise tomorrow. You will not have to come all the way back to the old hole to draw. Christ has promised it in so many words: the water He gives will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.
closingVerse: But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.
carry: When the old thirst comes back on Tuesday, where will you turn, now that Jesus has promised that the water He gives will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust tells a man his life is small. You get up in the dark, you work, you come home spent, and you do it again. The ground you tend belongs to someone else. The wages are thin. Whatever God is doing in the world, He is doing it somewhere else, through men with better words and cleaner records. You are a hand on the line, and the harvest is none of your business.

Under that lie sits a second one. It says that when God does move, He moves for the people who already belong — the church crowd, the right town, the decent families. Not for a woman with five husbands. Not for the outsider town down the road. Not for a desperate father whose boy is dying and who cannot find any faith in himself except the faith of a man who has run out of options.

Both lies keep your head down and your eyes on your boots. You stop expecting God to do anything near you, and you stop expecting Him to do much for you. The man who has believed them long enough has one honest prayer left, and it is a good one: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

In John 4:27–54 Jesus tells His men to do the opposite of what the dust says: lift up your eyes and look at the fields. A whole town comes out to Him on one woman’s word, and a nobleman’s son lives on one word from His mouth. The harvest belongs to Christ, He is Savior for the world, and the word He speaks does what it says. Neither the woman nor the town nor the father did the reaping. Christ did, and He still does.

sections.heading: A Town, a Field, and a Father
pulls: The dust keeps your head down and tells you the harvest is somewhere else. Jesus says lift up your eyes. The field is ripe, the work is His, and you have been sent to gather what He sowed.
paras: Last week left a woman at a well hearing I am he, the one who speaks to you. This week opens as the disciples walk back with food and find Him still talking with her. She leaves her water pot and goes into town. While she is gone, Jesus teaches His men about food and harvest, and the Samaritans come out to Him. Two days later He goes on into Galilee, back to Cana, where a nobleman from Capernaum meets Him with a dying son.

John calls that healing the second sign that Jesus did. Read the whole passage through at one sitting before you go further. Every scene asks what John’s whole book asks: who is this Man, and will you believe Him? The Samaritans answer that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world. The nobleman answers by turning around and walking home on nothing but a word.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: COME, SEE A MAN
paras: At this, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman. Yet nobody asks Him about it. They keep their questions in their pockets, and Jesus does not stop to explain Himself. He has nothing to apologize for. He was doing the Father’s business at the well while they were buying lunch in town.

Then John gives you a small detail with a lot of weight in it: the woman left her water pot. She came for one jar of water and found a spring, so she walks off without the jar. She has not stopped being thirsty. She has found something the jar could never carry. The thing that set the shape of her whole day now sits forgotten in the dust by Jacob’s well.

She goes back into town, among the people who know her history, and says: Come, see a man who told me everything that I did. Her sin has become her testimony. The thing she would once have kept quiet is the very thing she leads with, because it is the thing He knew and still did not walk away from. Her question is honest: Can this be the Christ? She does not have it all worked out. She has met Him, and she tells what happened.

They went out of the city, and were coming to him. That is how the harvest began in Sychar. Not with a trained preacher or a careful plan, but with a woman whose only credential was that Jesus had told her the truth about herself and given her water anyway. If you belong to Him, you carry the same credential.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: FOOD AND HARVEST
paras: Meanwhile the disciples hold out the food. Rabbi, eat. He says I have food to eat that you don’t know about, and they look at each other and wonder who slipped Him some bread. Then He tells them: My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work. He is truly a man. He got tired at the well and He needed bread like any man who has walked since morning. But what fed Him deepest was doing the Father’s will, and the Father’s will was the saving of sinners.

And He finished it. Near the end of this same Gospel He tells the Father, I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do, and from the cross He says It is finished. Every bit of the work that saves you was His food, and He did not leave a crumb of it for you to add.

Then He points at the fields. There are yet four months until the harvest — that was the saying, and any man who has worked the ground knows the waiting. Jesus says lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already. And while He speaks, a town is walking out toward Him.

I sent you to reap that for which you haven’t labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor. Here is grace in a field. The disciples did not plow Samaria. The Son sat tired by the well and sowed, and they walk in at harvest time to carry sheaves they did not grow. That is your place in His work too. Your part is to lift your eyes, gather what He grew, and rejoice together with the One who sowed.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE SAVIOR OF THE WORLD
pulls: Not the Savior of the decent, or of the right town and the right family. The Savior of the world — which means there is no man standing on the far side of His reach, and that includes you.
paras: From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman. One woman’s word, and many believe. Then they beg Him to stay with them. He stayed there two days. The Jew who was supposed to have no dealings with Samaritans sleeps under their roofs and eats at their tables. Many more believed because of his word.

Then they say to the woman, Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves. That is no insult to her. It is the harvest working the way it should. Her word brought them to Him. His word made them His. Every man’s faith has to come to that point. You cannot live on borrowed faith — your mother’s, your wife’s, your pastor’s. You need to hear Christ for yourself in His word, and He is willing to be heard.

And what they heard, they confess: this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world. Nowhere else in John’s Gospel is Jesus called Savior, and the men who say it are Samaritans. Men from the wrong people, who worshiped on the wrong mountain, said what His own countrymen would not. John has already told you that those who were his own didn’t receive him. These outsiders did.

He is not the Savior of the decent, or of the right town and the right family. He is the Savior of the world. That means no man stands on the far side of His reach. The woman with five husbands did not. The Samaritans everyone had written off did not. The man you have quietly given up on does not, and neither do you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: GO YOUR WAY
paras: After the two days He goes into Galilee. John reminds you that Jesus Himself said a prophet has no honor in his own country. The Galileans do welcome Him, but John tells you why: they had seen all the things that he did in Jerusalem at the feast. They welcomed a show. They had not yet bowed to a Savior.

Then comes the nobleman. His son is sick in Capernaum, at the point of death. The father comes up to Cana and begs Jesus to come down and heal him. Jesus answers with a hard word that takes in the whole crowd: Unless you see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe. The father does not argue. He just begs again: Sir, come down before my child dies.

Jesus does not go. He speaks. Go your way. Your son lives. And here is the hinge of the week: The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way. No sign in his hand. No Jesus walking beside him. Only a sentence, and he walks home on it.

On the road down, his servants meet him with the news. He asks the hour the boy turned. Yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him. That was the hour Jesus spoke. He believed, as did his whole house. This is what the sign shows you: the word of Jesus carries His life wherever He sends it. He does not need to be in the room. He speaks, and it is done. That same word reaches you. Christ is not sitting in your kitchen in the body, but He speaks in this book, and John says these are written, that you may believe.

stations.verse: Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.
stations.question: Jesus told disciples holding out bread, My food is to do the will of him who sent me — a work He finished for me; what plain duty in my week could I take up as food from my Father?
stations.live: Pick one plain duty you have resented — the early shift, the bills, the patient answer at home. Do it this week as food from your Father, and say: ‘This is His will, and He feeds me in it.’
body: Brōma is plain food, what a man eats. Most of the fifteen New Testament verses that use it mean it literally: food the crowds needed, food the law once sorted. A few times it is used of spiritual food — here, and where Paul writes I fed you with milk, not with meat.

Jesus takes the most daily word there is and fills it with the Father’s will. My food is to do the will of him who sent me. What kept Him going was not a meal but a mission, the saving of that woman. And He finished it, every bite of the work the Father gave Him.

The dust says you are what you consume: the praise, the paycheck, the feed on your phone. On that diet you will always be hungry. Christ ate the hard food of obedience to the end, so you can be fed from His finished work and find your Father’s will a meal rather than a weight.

stations.verse: Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest?’ Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.
stations.question: Jesus told men counting four months to lift up your eyes and look at the fields, while Samaritans were already walking out toward Him; whom near me have I decided is not ready to hear about Christ?
stations.gloss: harvest; the reaping, its season, its crop
stations.live: Name one person near you — at the shop, across the road, at your own table. Pray for him by name each morning this week, asking the Lord of the harvest to show you what He is already doing.
body: Therismos is harvest. It can mean the work of reaping, the season for it, or the crop standing in the field. Eight New Testament verses carry it, and in John 4:35 it is the reaping itself.

Elsewhere Jesus tells His men that the harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few, and sends them to pray to the Lord of the harvest. The harvest has an owner. It is His field, His seed, His rain and His sickle. He did the sowing. In Samaria He shows them a field already white while they were still counting months on their fingers.

The dust tells a man the harvest is someday, somewhere, and somebody else’s job. Jesus says already. The crop is His, and it is ripe. Lift your eyes from your own furrow, and you may find the reaping has already started walking out of town to meet you.

stations.verse: They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.
stations.question: Samaritans, the people Jews had no dealings with, heard Jesus for two days and confessed Him the Savior of the world; whose name have I quietly left outside that word world, even, some mornings, my own?
stations.live: Write down the name of the person you least expect to meet in heaven. Under it, write your own. Pray for both every day this week: ‘Savior of the world, You are able.’
body: Sōtēr means savior, deliverer, preserver. In the Greek Old Testament it renders the Hebrew words for saving, and the New Testament gives it to God and to Christ. Of the twenty-four New Testament verses that use it, only two call Him the Savior of the world: here, and in John’s first letter.

In John’s Gospel the word appears this once, and Samaritans say it. Men who worshiped on the wrong mountain heard Jesus for two days and confessed what His own people would not. He reaches past every line men draw, the lines you have drawn around yourself among them.
The dust says salvation is for the deserving and keeps a short list. Sōtēr will not stay on that list. A savior saves, and this Savior saves the world, which means He has room for a man like you.

stations.verse: For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.
stations.question: Jesus said a prophet has no honor in his own country, and Galilee welcomed Him for what it had seen at the feast; where has my long familiarity with Jesus left me wanting His works more than honoring Him?
stations.gloss: fatherland; one’s own country or hometown
stations.live: Read John 4 this week as if you had never heard of Jesus. Mark one thing He does that surprises you, and tell Him: ‘I have been too familiar. You are the Christ.’
body: Patris comes from the word for father. It is the land of one’s fathers: a man’s country, his home, his native town. Seven of its eight New Testament verses stand in the same setting, a prophet among his own people, and all four Gospels record the saying.

Familiar ground breeds a dull eye. In Luke, Jesus tells His hometown that no prophet is acceptable in his hometown. In Galilee the welcome came from men who had seen all the things that he did in Jerusalem, and honor that rests on a show is thin. A man can grow up near Christ — church every Sunday, a verse on the kitchen wall — and give Him less honor than Samaritans who met Him two days ago.

The dust says you know Jesus well enough already. But Scripture names another country. The fathers in the faith were seeking a country of their own. Christ took dishonor in His own country so you could be welcomed home into His.

stations.verse: Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way.
stations.question: Jesus told the nobleman, Go your way. Your son lives, and the man believed the word and walked home before he saw anything; which word of Christ am I refusing to walk on until I see it proved?
stations.live: Choose one promise of Christ from John 4 and write it on a card. Carry it in your pocket. When fear rises, take it out, read it, and keep walking: ‘He said it. It is so.’
body: Zaō means to live, to be alive; it can also mean to pass one’s life a certain way. It is one of the great verbs of the New Testament, found in 124 verses. Peter confesses Jesus as the Son of the living God, and Jesus offers the woman living water. In this chapter it marks a boy pulled back from the edge of death.

Three times in four verses it is spoken over the nobleman’s son: Your son lives from the lips of Jesus, Your child lives from the servants on the road, and the same words again as the father remembers the hour. Jesus never went down to Capernaum. He spoke, and the fever left at that hour. His word carries His life wherever He sends it.
The dust says you have to see before you can believe. The nobleman walked home with nothing but a word, and the word was enough. Christ says to you, Because I live, you will live also. Walk on that.

practices.title: SET DOWN ONE WATER POT
practices.body: The woman left her water pot. She had found something better than anything the jar could carry. Pick one thing you haul around every day out of habit and fear — the phone at the supper table, the third look at the bank balance, the late-night scrolling. Set it down for the week. Not as a penance to earn something. Do it as a man who has found living water and does not need to drag the old jar around anymore.

practices.title: TELL WHAT HE DID
practices.body: Her whole message was one line: He told me everything that I did. You do not need a polished story. Think through how Christ found you, what He knew about you, and how He did not walk away. Then tell one man this week, plainly, in under two minutes. Do not dress it up or trim the hard parts. A woman with a ruined name brought a whole town out to Jesus that way. The power was never in her telling. It was in the One she told about.

practices.title: EAT YOUR FATHER’S WILL
practices.body: Jesus said His food was to do the will of him who sent me. Pick the hardest ordinary duty of your week — the double shift, the talk with your wife you have been putting off, the bill you have not opened. Before you start it, say: ‘This is my Father’s will, and Christ has already finished the work that saves me.’ Then do the duty as a man who has been fed, not one who is starving for approval.

practices.title: LOOK UP AT THE FIELD
practices.body: Jesus told His men lift up your eyes and look at the fields. Once a day this week — at the fuel pump, over your lunch pail, at the gate on the way home — stop and look at the people around you. Ask the Lord of the harvest to show you one person He is already working on. Pray for that person by name every day, and before the week is out, speak one plain word of Christ to him. The field is His; you are only sent.

practices.title: WALK HOME ON A WORD
practices.body: The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way. Take the fear you carry most this week — the sick child, the shaky job, the cold marriage. Find one promise of Christ that speaks to it and write it down. Each time the fear comes back, read the promise and keep walking. You will not always be told the hour. You can trust the One who spoke, because His word reached Capernaum without Him.

title: Fields White for Harvest
subtitle: from dust to the Savior of the world
keyVerse: They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.

passage.text: At this, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why do you speak with her?”
So the woman left her water pot, went away into the city, and said to the people,
“Come, see a man who told me everything that I did. Can this be the Christ?”
They went out of the city, and were coming to him.
In the meanwhile, the disciples urged him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”
But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you don’t know about.”
The disciples therefore said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”
Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.
Don’t you say, ‘There are yet four months until the harvest?’ Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.
He who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit to eternal life; that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together.
For in this the saying is true, ‘One sows, and another reaps.’
I sent you to reap that for which you haven’t labored. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”
From that city many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything that I did.”
So when the Samaritans came to him, they begged him to stay with them. He stayed there two days.
Many more believed because of his word.
They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.”
After the two days he went out from there and went into Galilee.
For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.
So when he came into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen all the things that he did in Jerusalem at the feast, for they also went to the feast.
Jesus came therefore again to Cana of Galilee, where he made the water into wine. There was a certain nobleman whose son was sick at Capernaum.
When he heard that Jesus had come out of Judea into Galilee, he went to him, and begged him that he would come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
Jesus therefore said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you will in no way believe.”
The nobleman said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”
Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him, and he went his way.
As he was now going down, his servants met him and reported, saying “Your child lives!”
So he inquired of them the hour when he began to get better. They said therefore to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him.”
So the father knew that it was at that hour in which Jesus said to him, “Your son lives.” He believed, as did his whole house.
This is again the second sign that Jesus did, having come out of Judea into Galilee.
