stationsIntro: The second half of John 4 turns on food, harvest, a title, a hometown, and life itself. Read each verse before you answer, keep your answer plain, and let each word turn you back to what Christ has already done.
lifeIntro: Christ finished the work His Father gave Him, and He is the Savior of the world. His word still gives life where He cannot be seen. A man sent into a field already ripe can live this week by these five practices.
lifePulls: The woman left her water pot. The Samaritans heard Him for themselves. The father walked home on a word. In every scene Jesus does the work, and men simply believe Him and go.
prayer: Father, You sent Your Son to do Your will and finish Your work, and He finished it. Thank You that Jesus is the Savior of the world, and so the Savior of a man like me. I confess I have kept my eyes on the ground and called the harvest someone else’s business. I confess I have wanted signs before I would trust Your word. Lift my eyes to the field You have already made ready. Give me the plain courage of the woman who told her town to come and see. Teach me to walk home on Your word, even when I cannot see the hour it works. Thank You that Your word reaches where I cannot see, and gives life there. Make Your will my food this week, and feed me from the finished work of Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You sent Your Son to do Your will and finish Your work, and He finished it.
Thank You that Jesus is the Savior of the world, and so the Savior of a man like me.
I confess I have kept my eyes on the ground and called the harvest someone else’s business.
I confess I have wanted signs before I would trust Your word.
Lift my eyes to the field You have already made ready.
Give me the plain courage of the woman who told her town to come and see.
Teach me to walk home on Your word, even when I cannot see the hour it works.
Thank You that Your word reaches where I cannot see, and gives life there.
Make Your will my food this week, and feed me from the finished work of Christ.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: A woman left her water pot and told a town what Jesus knew about her. The Samaritans heard Him for themselves and called Him the Savior of the world. A father begged for his dying son and walked home on one sentence. Christ finished the Father’s work, and His word still gives life at a distance. Lift your eyes. The field is His, and it is ripe.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, the way Jesus told His men to lift theirs. Lift them from the furrow you have been staring into all year. Lift them from the fuel bill on the counter and the son who will not talk to you. Lift them from the short list of people you have decided God will never reach. Look at the field. It is whiter than you thought, and it is not yours. It belongs to the One who sowed it.

He sowed it with His own labor. He walked to Sychar tired, sat in the dust by Jacob’s well, and waited for a woman no one else was waiting for. He spent two days under Samaritan roofs. He took the Father’s will as His food and did not stop until He had eaten all of it. When He said It is finished, the work was done — every hard row of it plowed and planted by a Man who never once worked for His own name.

So you do not have to carry the year on your back. You walk into a field He has already worked, and you gather fruit you did not grow. The sower and the reaper get to rejoice together. Your clumsy word to a neighbor, your prayer for your son, your plain witness at the shop — none of it has to make anything grow. He gives the growth. He is not the Savior of one town or one kind of man. He is the Savior of the world, and no man stands past His reach, you included.

And when fear has you by the throat, remember the father on the road down to Capernaum. He had no sign in his hand. He had a sentence: Go your way. Your son lives. He went, and the word had already done its work before he got home. The One who spoke that sentence walked out of His own grave alive, and He speaks over you now: Because I live, you will live also. You will not always see the hour it works. Walk home on that word anyway. You will find, as he did, that the word got home before you.
closingVerse: They said to the woman, “Now we believe, not because of your speaking; for we have heard for ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.
carry: The Samaritans moved from the woman’s word to we have heard for ourselves; where this week will you sit down with Christ’s own word until you can say the same of the Savior of the world?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: A man can lie in the same place so long he stops calling it a place. It is just where he is. The same sin meets you at the same hour. The same cold quiet sits in the house after supper. The same grudge against your brother gets fed every time his name comes up. You quit asking whether it could change somewhere around year twelve, and now the mat has your shape pressed into it.

The dust has a theory about men like you. It says help is out there, but it goes to the quick ones — the man with friends, the man with money, the man who can get to the water first. It says your trouble is position. If you could get closer, move faster, find someone strong enough to carry you, you might have a shot. So you lie there and plan, and you watch other men step in ahead of you, and the planning turns into its own kind of sickness.

Thirty-eight years is a long time to cling to the dust. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Look at how that prayer ends. Not according to my speed. Not according to the water. According to Your word. That is how the man at Bethesda was raised. Jesus did not get him into the pool. He spoke, and the man stood up. He had no faith worth naming and no legs to bring. He had a word spoken over him, and that was enough.

sections.heading: A Feast, a Pool, and the Sabbath
pulls: The man at the pool had a plan for his healing, and the plan had failed him for thirty-eight years. Jesus did not improve the plan. He spoke one word, and the man stood up.
paras: John has just told you of a nobleman who took Jesus at His word and went home to find his son alive (4:50). Now there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. John does not name the feast. He names the place: a pool by the sheep gate, called Bethesda, having five porches. Under those roofs lay a great multitude of those who were sick, blind, lame, or paralyzed. It was a crowded, waiting place, full of men who had run out of options.

Out of that whole crowd Jesus goes to one man. He heals him with a word, on a Sabbath, and the healing starts a fight that runs to the end of the chapter. Read 5:1–18 through slowly this week and watch where John keeps your eye. Not on the water. Not on the man’s faith, which is thin. On Jesus — what He sees, what He says, and who He claims to be. John wrote his signs that you may believe (20:31), and this one is written for the man who has been down a long time.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: HE SAW HIM LYING THERE
paras: A certain man was there who had been sick for thirty-eight years. John gives you the number and almost nothing else. No name. No hometown. No word on how it started. Only the years, stacked like cordwood against a wall — long enough for a boy to be born, grow up, marry, and bury his father, while this man lay on the same stones.

Then the first move belongs to Jesus. When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time. The man did not call out. He did not push to the front. Jesus saw him, and Jesus knew. John told you back in chapter 2 that the Lord knew what was in man, and here that knowing comes down to one porch and one mat. Before the man says a word, he is known all the way to the bone. So are you.

Then Jesus asks, Do you want to be made well? It sounds like a strange thing to ask a man who has waited half a lifetime beside a pool. It is not strange at all. Long sickness becomes a way of life. A man learns how to live on the mat, how to talk about it, what to expect from people and what not to. The question carries no test of merit. It puts a finger on the place where the man quit hoping.
That is grace, and it comes first. Jesus chose this man before the man said one useful thing. He deals the same way with you. The first move in your rescue was never yours.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: NO ONE TO PUT ME IN
paras: Listen to the answer. Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, but while I’m coming, another steps down before me. Jesus asked a yes-or-no question. The man hands Him a report on the system. He believes the water is the cure, the race is the rule, and he is losing the race. All he can see is what he lacks: a helper, a head start, legs.

You know that answer because you have given it. Ask a man if he wants to be free of the bottle and he will tell you about his father. Ask him if he wants peace with his wife and he will tell you what she said in March. The dust always keeps an explanation ready. It is never quite a no. It is a list of reasons why yes is out of reach. Fill in your own list; you know it by heart.

Jesus does not argue with the list. He does not offer to help with the pool. He does not hand the man three steps toward stronger legs. He says, Arise, take up your mat, and walk. Then comes the shortest report in the story: Immediately, the man was made well, and took up his mat and walked. The word did what it said. Bone and sinew idle for thirty-eight years obeyed a voice the man had never heard before that day.

Notice what the man brought. Not faith in Jesus; he did not yet know who Jesus was (5:13). Not effort; he could not stand. He brought the mat, and the mat was only proof of how long he had been down. The healing was all Christ’s, and so is yours.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THEY SAW THE MAT
pulls: Religion without Christ sees the mat on the Sabbath and misses the man who is walking. Grace sees a dead thing standing up and asks only one question: who made it stand?
paras: Now it was the Sabbath on that day. John drops that line like a stone into a stock tank, and the rings run all the way to verse 47. A man who had not walked in thirty-eight years is walking through Jerusalem with his bedding under his arm, and the first thing the religious men notice is the bedding. Not one of them asks how. It is the Sabbath. It is not lawful for you to carry the mat. When they do ask who, it is only to find the man who told him to break the rule.

That is what religion without Christ always sees. It sees the rule bent and misses the man restored. It counts what you carried and never asks who made you able to carry it. There is a version of you that does this at church, at home, to your own sons — quick to name the mat on the Sabbath, slow to stand amazed that a dead thing is walking.

The healed man has one answer, and it is a good one. He who made me well said to me, ‘Take up your mat and walk.’ He does not defend himself. He points to the word that raised him. He cannot even give them a name, because he who was healed didn’t know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, a crowd being in the place.

That should steady you. The man’s healing did not hang on how much he understood. It hung on the One who spoke. You will not be able to answer every sharp question a clever man throws at your faith. You can always say this much: He made me well, and He told me to walk. No one can argue you out of that.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: MY FATHER IS STILL WORKING
paras: Afterward Jesus found him in the temple. Jesus withdrew, and then He came looking. That is the second time in this story the Lord takes the first step. He found the man, and He said, Behold, you are made well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.

Hear the order. First, you are made well — a finished fact. Then, sin no more. Jesus does not say, quit sinning and I will heal you. He heals, and then He tells the healed man how to walk. The command rides on the gift. That is the order of the whole gospel. And there is something worse than thirty-eight years on a mat. Before this chapter is done Jesus will speak of the resurrection of judgment (5:29). The legs were mended in a moment. The man’s deeper need was a Savior from sin, and the Savior had come looking for him.

Then the fight sharpens. The leaders persecuted Jesus, and sought to kill him, because he did these things on the Sabbath. Jesus answers with one line: My Father is still working, so I am working, too. The Father did not stop keeping the world on the seventh day. Rain still fell on the Sabbath. Calves were still born. Jesus says He does that same work, alongside His Father, and on this Sabbath He was doing it beside a pool.

His enemies understood Him exactly: he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Jesus does not take it back. He does not soften it. The man carrying his mat through the city had been made well by God Himself, walking the porches of Bethesda in human flesh.

stations.verse: Now in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, there is a pool, which is called in Hebrew, “Bethesda”, having five porches.
stations.question: Bethesda’s porches were full of sick men waiting for the moving of the water, and Jesus walked past the water to one man; what am I waiting on to fix me, when Christ has already come to where I lie?
stations.live: Name the pool you have been waiting beside this year. Then turn from it toward Christ, who comes to men who cannot get to the water, and say it plainly: ‘You came to the porch. You came to me.’
body: Kolymbēthra is a plain word for a pool; properly, a swimming pool. It turns up only three times in the New Testament, and John owns all three: twice for Bethesda in this chapter and once for the pool of Siloam (9:7). The Greek Old Testament uses it for the Hebrew berekah, a pool.

Bethesda was a gathering place for hopeless men. They lay under its porches with their eyes on the water, and this man tells you what he was waiting for: the water stirred, and a chance to be first. The pool was the center of their world. Jesus never sends this man into it. He walks past the water to the man.

The dust wants you lying beside something — a program, a better year, the right person to carry you — waiting on a stir. The pool did not heal anyone in this story. The Word who came to the porch did, and He came to a man who could not reach the water.

stations.verse: A certain man was there who had been sick for thirty-eight years.
stations.question: John gives this man no name, only thirty-eight years of sickness, and Jesus knew that he had been sick for a long time; what long weakness of mine have I stopped bringing to Him because I assume He has stopped noticing it?
stations.live: Tell one man you trust about the weakness you have quietly moved into — the one you quit praying about. Then pray over it together, out loud, as men whose high priest feels it with them.
body: Astheneia means weakness, frailty, sickness — a body or a man without strength. It turns up in twenty-three New Testament verses. John’s phrase is worth slowing down for: the man had spent thirty-eight years in his weakness, the same way Paul says he came to Corinth in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling.

Weakness was not only something this man had. It was where he lived. A man can move into his weakness the way he moves into a rented house — learns where the drafts are, quits asking for repairs. Yet Scripture uses this same word for the very place Christ shows His strength: my power is made perfect in weakness.

The dust says your weakness puts you out of reach. But Christ is no high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities. He came to the stones where weak men lay, and He knew this one through and through before the man ever spoke.

stations.verse: When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, he asked him, “Do you want to be made well?
stations.question: When Jesus asked a man thirty-eight years down, Do you want to be made well? he answered with reasons; what reasons do I hand Christ instead of a plain yes about my own long sickness?
stations.live: Answer Jesus’ question this week without a list of reasons. Say it plainly, once in the morning and once before you sleep: ‘Yes, Lord. I want to be made well.’ Do not add a word after it.
body: Hygiēs means sound, whole, healthy. Of its eleven New Testament appearances, six belong to John, and five of those are packed into this one chapter. When Jesus looks back on this healing in 7:23, He says He made a man completely healthy on the Sabbath. Not patched. Whole.

So the question at the pool is bigger than it sounds. Do you want to be made well? asks, do you want to be whole? Peter used the same word after a lame man walked at the temple: this man stands here before you whole in him — whole in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.

The dust wants you to settle for managing — a little less sick, a little better at hiding it. Christ is after the whole man, body and soul. He does not trim the edges of a sickness. He says one word, and a man who could not stand is walking home with his bedding under his arm.

stations.verse: Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.
stations.question: Jesus did not help the man to the pool; He said, Arise, take up your mat, and walk, and His word gave the legs it commanded; where is He calling me to stand on His word before I feel strong enough?
stations.live: Name your mat. This week, pick it up in one concrete act of walking: the call you dodged, the debt you start paying down, the apology you owe. Then say it: ‘He who made me well told me to walk.’
body: Krabattos is a camp bed, a pallet — a poor man’s bedding, light enough to roll up and carry. It was a Macedonian word. Eleven New Testament verses use it, and four of those fall in John 5:8–11, as the mat goes from under the man to under his arm to the middle of an argument.

Mark uses the same word for the paralyzed man let down through a roof, and Jesus’ command there runs close to this one: arise, take up your mat, and go to your house. In both places the mat changes jobs. For years it had carried the man. Now the man carries it.

The dust says the mat is who you are — the drinker, the angry one, the man who always quits. Christ does not leave the mat lying there as a monument. He tells you to pick it up and walk, carrying the proof of what He has done.

stations.verse: For this cause therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
stations.question: The leaders wanted Jesus dead because He called God his own Father, making himself equal with God, and He never took it back; how would my prayers change if I came to Jesus as God Himself, not a good man I admire?
stations.gloss: equal; the same in size, number, or quality
stations.live: Speak to Jesus this week as God, not only about Him. Begin each prayer with one plain line and mean it: ‘Lord Jesus, You are equal with the Father, and You made me well.’
body: Isos means equal — the same in size, number, or quality. It is used of a gift given alike, of testimonies that would not line up, and of all-day hands who grumbled about the late hires, you have made them equal to us.

The leaders heard Jesus call God his own Father and understood the claim: making himself equal with God. Paul uses this word for the same truth from the other side. Christ, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped. He did not grab at what was already His. He came down into the dust.
The dust says Jesus was a fine man with good advice. His enemies knew better than that. Only God could do what was done at Bethesda, and only God can raise a man like you.

practices.title: NAME THE POOL
practices.body: Christ walked past Bethesda’s water to a man who could not reach it. Write down what you have been waiting on to fix you — a new job, a better season at home, a surge of willpower, the right man to carry you. Read 5:7 next to it. Then cross it out and write one line underneath: Jesus came to me. Keep the page on the dash where you will see it before work every morning this week.

practices.title: ANSWER WITHOUT THE LIST
practices.body: Jesus asked, Do you want to be made well? and the man answered with reasons. Take one place where you have quit hoping — the temper, the lust, the coldness toward your wife. When you pray about it this week, kneel if you can, and do not explain. Do not report on the system. Tell Him yes, and ask Him to speak. He healed a man who had thirty-eight years of explanations, and He did not ask for one of them.

practices.title: PICK UP THE MAT
practices.body: The man’s first act as a well man was to carry what used to carry him. Choose one concrete act this week that shows you are not lying down anymore: pour out the bottle, delete the app, call your brother, set the alarm for Sunday and be in the pew. Do it because Christ has made you well, not to get Him to. Carry the mat where people can see it, and when they ask, tell them who made you well.

practices.title: STOP COUNTING MATS
practices.body: The leaders watched a man walk and complained about his bedding. Christ has been patient with you; be slow to keep score on others. When a man near you is changing — a son, a new believer, the neighbor who just started coming to church — and you catch yourself listing what he still gets wrong, stop. Say out loud what Christ has done in him. Thank God for it in front of him, and let him hear you do it.

practices.title: WALK BACK INTO THE TEMPLE
practices.body: Jesus found the man in the temple and said Sin no more after He had already made him well. Pick the sin that keeps pulling you back to the mat. Fight it this week as a man already healed, not as a man trying to earn a healing. When you fall, run toward prayer and toward His people, not away. The One who found him there knows exactly where to find you, and He comes looking.

title: Take Up Your Mat
subtitle: from dust to a man made well
keyVerse: Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.

passage.text: After these things, there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
Now in Jerusalem by the sheep gate, there is a pool, which is called in Hebrew, “Bethesda”, having five porches.
In these lay a great multitude of those who were sick, blind, lame, or paralyzed, waiting for the moving of the water;
for an angel went down at certain times into the pool and stirred up the water. Whoever stepped in first after the stirring of the water was healed of whatever disease he had.
A certain man was there who had been sick for thirty-eight years.
When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, he asked him, “Do you want to be made well?”
The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, but while I’m coming, another steps down before me.”
Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.”
Immediately, the man was made well, and took up his mat and walked. Now it was the Sabbath on that day.
So the Jews said to him who was cured, “It is the Sabbath. It is not lawful for you to carry the mat.”
He answered them, “He who made me well said to me, ‘Take up your mat and walk.’”
Then they asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ‘Take up your mat and walk’?”
But he who was healed didn’t know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, a crowd being in the place.
Afterward Jesus found him in the temple, and said to him, “Behold, you are made well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.”
The man went away, and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.
For this cause the Jews persecuted Jesus, and sought to kill him, because he did these things on the Sabbath.
But Jesus answered them, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.”
For this cause therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.

stationsIntro: This week’s words run from the water under the porches to the claim that turned Jerusalem against Him. Read each verse first, answer the question as yourself, and let the Greek push you back toward the One who spoke.
lifeIntro: Jesus saw the man, spoke the word, and found him again in the temple. Every step in this story starts with Him. None of what follows earns a healing; the man was well before he took a step. These are ways to walk on the legs He has given you.
lifePulls: Jesus did not ask the man to get himself to the water. He came to the mat, spoke one word, and then went looking for him again in the temple. Grace takes the first step, and the second.
prayer: Father, You saw me lying there before I ever called out to You. You knew how long I had been in the dust, and You did not pass me by. Your Son came to the place where I could not get up, and He spoke. I confess the pools I have trusted and the lists of reasons I keep ready. Make me whole, Lord, not patched. Give me legs to carry the mat in plain view and walk where You send me. Keep me from counting other men’s mats when I should be praising what You have done. Find me again when I wander, as You found him in the temple. Thank You that Jesus is equal with You, and that His word does what it says. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You saw me lying there before I ever called out to You.
You knew how long I had been in the dust, and You did not pass me by.
Your Son came to the place where I could not get up, and He spoke.
I confess the pools I have trusted and the lists of reasons I keep ready.
Make me whole, Lord, not patched.
Give me legs to carry the mat in plain view and walk where You send me.
Keep me from counting other men’s mats when I should be praising what You have done.
Find me again when I wander, as You found him in the temple.
Thank You that Jesus is equal with You, and that His word does what it says.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: A man lay thirty-eight years beside a pool, sure that healing went to whoever reached the water first. Jesus saw him, asked one question, and spoke one word, and the man stood up and carried his mat. The leaders saw a broken rule. Jesus saw a man made whole, and called God His own Father while doing it. Quit waiting on the water. The One equal with God has already spoken.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the One who came to the porch. He came when you could not come to Him. He came when there was no one to put you in the water. He came when the years had stacked up and the hope had drained out of you, and He knew how long it had been before you said a word. You did not find Him. He saw you lying there. He picked one man out of a great multitude, and He has not overlooked you.

The dust has told you that healing goes to the quick and the strong and the well connected — that you are one more body on the stones, watching other men step in ahead of you. But the water healed no one at Bethesda. A voice did. Arise, take up your mat, and walk. The Word who was with God in the beginning spoke into thirty-eight years of wasted sinew, and the sinew obeyed. He did not ask for a running start. He asked for nothing the man did not have, and then He gave him legs.

And He did not stop there. Jesus slipped into the crowd, and then He went looking. Afterward Jesus found him in the temple. The Lord who heals a man comes back to finish what He began — to tell him he is well, to warn him off the worse thing, to make sure the healed man knows whose word raised him. He does not drop you after the first mercy. He finds you again. He knows the hospital hallway, the back field, the parked truck where you sit with the engine off and cannot pray. He will come looking there too.

So carry the mat this week in plain view. Let men complain about it if they want to. You have one answer, and it is enough: He who made me well told me to walk. The Son who said My Father is still working, so I am working, too has not laid down His tools, and the work in His hands includes you. He spoke one word at Bethesda, and a man thirty-eight years down stood up. Then He went looking for that man and found him in the temple. The One equal with God has spoken that word over you, and He will find you again.
closingVerse: Jesus said to him, “Arise, take up your mat, and walk.
carry: What would it look like on Tuesday to take up the mat you have lain on for years, simply because Jesus said, Arise, take up your mat, and walk?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men live as if court were still in session. You wake up, and the case against you opens again. Yesterday’s temper is entered as evidence. So is the thing on the phone, the money you shaded, the prayer you skipped. You do not know when the verdict comes. You only know it has not come yet, and that every day you are either building your defense or losing ground. Some nights you lie awake rehearsing your side of it.

The dust tells you that is simply what faith feels like — a long trial with a decent lawyer. Then it stacks a second lie on the first. It says you can honor God in a general way and keep His Son at arm’s length: a prayer before the ballgame, church at Christmas, the name of Jesus left politely out of it. And it tells you a third: that the Bible is a ladder, and the more rungs you climb, the closer you get.

Set the anchor verse beside this chapter. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) A man face down in the dust asks for life, and he asks for it by a word. In 5:24 Jesus gives that word, and it does not open a trial. It closes one. He who hears and believes has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life. The man at Bethesda got his legs back. This week the Son offers you something larger than legs.

sections.heading: Jesus Answers the Charge
pulls: The dust says court opens again every morning. Jesus says the man who hears His word and believes has already passed out of death into life. The case is closed, and he is standing on the far bank.
paras: The man at the pool walked, and Jerusalem’s leaders wanted Jesus dead, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God (5:18). Last week ended there. This week Jesus answers the charge. He does not back away from it. He spends twenty-nine verses making it plainer. Equal with God? Yes — and here is what that means for a man in the dust.

Read it in two movements. In 5:19–30 Jesus tells you what the Son does: whatever the Father does, He does; He gives life; He holds all judgment; He calls the dead. In 5:31–47 He calls His witnesses — John the Baptist, His own works, the Father, and the Scriptures Moses wrote. This is the last week of Part One, and it ends where John wants every page to end: on whether you will come to Him and live. Read the whole passage in one sitting before you start the questions.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE SON DOES LIKEWISE
paras: The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. Do not hear that as weakness. Hear it as union. The Son never works on His own, apart from the Father, and the Father never works apart from Him: whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise. Equal, one, and never at odds.

Underneath it all is love. For the Father has affection for the Son, and shows him all things that he himself does. The Son is held in the Father’s affection and shown everything, and He promises greater works than these, that you may marvel. A crippled man walking is not the top of it. Raising the dead is. And this is the love the Son brings you into. You are not let in as a hired man at the back door. You are brought in by the Son Himself, and the Father receives you for His sake.

For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life to whom he desires. Life is the Son’s to give, and He gives it as He wills. That is good news for a dead man, because a dead man has no will that works. Then judgment: the Father has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son, even as they honor the Father.

There is no honoring a general God who keeps His Son at a distance. He who doesn’t honor the Son doesn’t honor the Father who sent him. A man can bow his head before the meal at the county fair and still be outside. The only Father there is comes to you through the Son, and the Son has come all the way to you.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: PASSED OUT OF DEATH INTO LIFE
paras: Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. Read the tense. Not will have, if he holds out. Has. Eternal life is not a prize at the end of a long road. It is a present possession, handed over the moment a dead man hears and believes.

Then two more verbs, and both are settled. He doesn’t come into judgment. The court that convenes every morning in your head has no case left on the docket, because Christ took the verdict on Himself. And he has passed out of death into life. That crossing is already made. You stand on the far bank now, with the river at your back.

The hour comes, and now is, when the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live. Graves come later in the chapter. Here Jesus speaks of men who walk around dead in their sins, and of the voice that raises them now. Paul says the same thing to the Ephesians: You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins. No man ever listened his way into life by his own strength. The voice does the raising.

How can the Son do this? For as the Father has life in himself, even so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself. He has life the way a spring has water, rising from within. That is why His word to you is no mere advice. It carries His own life into a dead man. And He is Judge because he is a son of man. The One who took on flesh and walked in the dust is the One who will sit on the bench.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ALL WHO ARE IN THE TOMBS
pulls: These men searched the Scriptures for what they had to do and never saw what God had promised to do. The Bible is not a ladder for climbing to God. It is a witness, and every page points to the Son.
paras: Don’t marvel at this, for the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice. Now Jesus speaks of graves. The voice that raises dead souls today will one day raise dead bodies. There is one return of Christ and one resurrection of the dead, the righteous and the wicked together, called out of the ground by the same voice.

Those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment. Do not turn that into a ledger. Jesus has just told you that the man who believes has already passed into life. Good works on that day are not the price of life. They are what life looks like after it has been growing in a man. A pear tree does not come alive by bearing pears; the pears show it was alive.

And look who sits as Judge. I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous. His verdict is right because He seeks His Father’s will and not His own. The Judge on that day will be the Son who walked up to a mat at Bethesda. If you belong to Him, the One on the bench is the One who already stood in your place and bore what you were owed.

That takes the dread out of the last day for a believer without taking the weight out of it. It will be real. Every grave will open, every family plot and every unmarked field. But a man who has heard His voice now will hear that same voice then, and he will know it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THESE TESTIFY ABOUT ME
paras: Then Jesus calls witnesses. John the Baptist first: He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light. Men enjoyed John for a season and moved on. Then the works: the very works that I do, testify about me. Then the Father Himself, who sent me, has testified about me.

Then the Scriptures. You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. These men knew their Bibles. They searched them for what they had to do to be saved and never saw what God had promised to do to save them. They held the map and missed the country. A man can read his Bible every morning for forty years and do the same.

Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life. That is the saddest line in the chapter. The trouble was not a lack of light. It was a will turned away. Jesus names the root: How can you believe, who receive glory from one another? A man who lives for the nod of other men — the crew, the deacons, the regulars at the parts counter — cannot rest his whole weight on Christ.

Then the last turn. Don’t think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope. The law they leaned on would testify against them. But Moses wrote about me, Jesus says, and Christ did not come as prosecutor. Read the Scriptures to find Him, and the same Moses who accuses will point you to the One who carries the charge away.

stations.verse: For the Father has affection for the Son, and shows him all things that he himself does. He will show him greater works than these, that you may marvel.
stations.question: Jesus promised men plotting His death greater works than these, that you may marvel — giving life to the dead; what life has the Son given me that I have quit marveling at?
stations.live: Write down one thing Christ has done for you that you have quit marveling at — a sin forgiven, a habit broken, a child spared. Read it aloud before supper one night this week, and thank Him for it by name.
body: Thaumazō means to marvel, to wonder, to wonder at. It shows up in forty-three New Testament verses, six of them in John. Crowds marvel at Jesus again and again. The Gospels also say He Himself marveled — at a centurion’s faith (Luke 7:9) and at the unbelief in His hometown (Mark 6:6).

In this chapter Jesus turns the word two ways. He promises greater works than these, that you may marvel, and then He says, Don’t marvel at this. Not because it is small, but because something larger is coming: the dead in the tombs hearing His voice. Wonder is meant to go somewhere. It is meant to end in belief.

The dust makes a man bored with grace. A healed body and a raised soul turn into old news by Thursday. But Paul uses this same word for the day Christ comes back, when He will be admired among all those who have believed. The wonder you lost is coming back, and it will not wear off.

stations.verse: For the Father judges no one, but he has given all judgment to the Son.
stations.question: Jesus says the Father has given all judgment to the Son, the same Son who promises that the believer doesn’t come into judgment; when my failures stand up and accuse me this week, whose verdict do I listen to?
stations.live: When the old charges come this week, answer them with the verdict, not your record. Say it out loud if you have to: ‘All judgment is given to the Son, and in Him I do not come into judgment.’
body: Krisis comes from krinō. Its range runs from a separating, to a decision or judgment, and above all to God’s judgment. It stands in forty-six New Testament verses, eleven of them in John, and five of John’s land in this one stretch of chapter 5 (5:22, 24, 27, 29, 30).

Jesus says the Father has given all judgment to the Son. Two verses later He says the man who believes doesn’t come into judgment. Put those side by side. The One who holds every verdict is the One who promises you will not stand in the dock. He holds the gavel, and He took the sentence. No higher court sits above Him to overturn it.

The dust keeps the courtroom open in your head, calling witnesses every night. But John writes that believers may have boldness in the day of judgment. Boldness, not because your record is clean, but because the Judge is your Savior and He has already ruled.

stations.verse: Most certainly I tell you, the hour comes, and now is, when the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live.
stations.question: Jesus says the hour now is, when the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; where have I treated His word as advice for living men rather than the voice that raised me from the dead?
stations.live: Read John 5:19–29 aloud once this week, slowly, the way you would read a letter with your name on the envelope. Then sit quiet a few minutes before you get up, and say: ‘I was dead, Lord Jesus, and You called me.’
body: Phōnē is a voice — a person speaking or crying out — and at times the sound of a thing, like the wind in 3:8. It is a common word, found in one hundred twenty-eight New Testament verses, fifteen of them in John. In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly translates the Hebrew word for voice.

John hangs life and death on it. The dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live. Later Jesus says His sheep hear my voice, and at a friend’s tomb he cried with a loud voice, and the dead man came out.

The dust says God went quiet long ago, and that a man like you is too far gone to hear Him. But dead men do not need good ears. They need a voice strong enough to raise them. The Son has that voice, and He has not stopped speaking through His word.

stations.verse: He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.
stations.question: The crowds were willing to rejoice for a while in John’s light but never followed it to Jesus; which man God has used as a lamp to me have I enjoyed without letting him bring me to Christ?
stations.live: Thank God this week for one man who has been a lamp to you. Then tell that man plainly that you are following the Light he pointed you to, and thank him for pointing.
body: Lychnos is a lamp — a portable one, usually set on a stand. It occurs fourteen times in the New Testament and only here in John. Scripture sets lamp against sun in Revelation 22:5, where in the city to come they need no lamp light or sun light.

Jesus calls John the Baptist the burning and shining lamp. A good lamp. But a lamp is lit by another hand, and it burns down. John himself was not the light, but was sent that he might testify about the light. Men warmed themselves at him for a while and then drifted off.

The dust wants you living from lamp to lamp — a good sermon, a strong month, a man you admire. Thank God for every lamp He has set along your road. But Scripture says the city’s lamp is the Lamb, and that Lamp never burns down.

stations.verse: Don’t think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope.
stations.question: Jesus told men who had set your hope on Moses that Moses would accuse them, for he wrote about me; where am I resting my hope on my own law-keeping instead of on the Christ the law points to?
stations.live: When the accusation comes this week, do not argue your record. Point past yourself to Christ and say it: ‘The accuser has been thrown down. Christ died and was raised, and He speaks for me.’
body: Katēgoreō means to make accusation, to accuse — sometimes in general, often before a judge. Most of the twenty-one New Testament verses that use it come from courtrooms and charge sheets: men accusing Jesus before Pilate, Paul’s enemies accusing him before governors. John uses it only here.

And here Jesus surprises His hearers. Don’t think that I will accuse you to the Father. He did not come to prosecute. The accuser is Moses — the law they trusted, which, read rightly, pointed to Christ all along. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me.

The dust keeps a prosecutor on call, and Scripture names him the accuser of our brothers. But that same verse says he has been thrown down. The charge is answered. Paul asks, Who is he who condemns? and answers with a Person: It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead.

practices.title: CLOSE THE COURTROOM
practices.body: Christ has said the believer doesn’t come into judgment. Write John 5:24 on a card and keep it in your shirt pocket or your wallet. When the case against you opens again — at three in the morning, after the argument, after the fall — take out the card and read it aloud. Do not reopen the trial yourself. The Judge has spoken, and He spoke for you. Keep the card until its corners wear soft.

practices.title: HONOR THE SON BY NAME
practices.body: The Father is honored only where the Son is honored, and the Son has given you His name to pray in. This week, pray to the Father in the name of Jesus on purpose, not as a closing tag. When you give thanks at the table, say His name plainly. When someone near you talks about God in a general way, speak of Jesus by name — kindly, without a sermon. A man who has life in the Son can say so without apology.

practices.title: READ FOR HIM
practices.body: Jesus said the Scriptures testify about me. Take one Old Testament passage this week — Genesis 3, Psalm 22, or Isaiah 53. Before you read, ask where Christ is in it. After you read, write one sentence on what God promises to do in Him, not what you are supposed to do. Read the way a man listens for one voice he knows in a crowded room. Mark every place you find Him.

practices.title: STOP FEEDING ON PRAISE
practices.body: Jesus asked, How can you believe, who receive glory from one another? In Christ you already have the Father’s approval. Name the person whose nod you work for — a boss, your father, the men on the crew. This week, do one good thing no one will see: fix what nobody will notice, pay what no one will thank you for. Do it for the Father, who sees it, and let His approval be enough.

practices.title: LISTEN FOR THE VOICE
practices.body: The dead hear the Son’s voice and live, and you have heard it. Set aside ten minutes on three mornings this week before the house wakes. Read John 5:19–30 aloud. Then be quiet. Do not rush to fill the silence with requests. Let the Son speak through what He has said, and answer Him with one sentence of thanks for the life He has already given. Then go to work as a man who is alive, because you are.

title: The Son Gives Life
subtitle: from dust to passing from death to life
keyVerse: Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.

passage.text: Jesus therefore answered them, “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.
For the Father has affection for the Son, and shows him all things that he himself does. He will show him greater works than these, that you may marvel.
For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son also gives life to whom he desires.
For the Father judges no one, but he has given all judgment to the Son,
that all may honor the Son, even as they honor the Father. He who doesn’t honor the Son doesn’t honor the Father who sent him.
“Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.
Most certainly I tell you, the hour comes, and now is, when the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live.
For as the Father has life in himself, even so he gave to the Son also to have life in himself.
He also gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is a son of man.
Don’t marvel at this, for the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice,
and will come out; those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.
I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.
“If I testify about myself, my witness is not valid.
It is another who testifies about me. I know that the testimony which he testifies about me is true.
You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth.
But the testimony which I receive is not from man. However, I say these things that you may be saved.
He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.
But the testimony which I have is greater than that of John, for the works which the Father gave me to accomplish, the very works that I do, testify about me, that the Father has sent me.
The Father himself, who sent me, has testified about me. You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his form.
You don’t have his word living in you, because you don’t believe him whom he sent.
“You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me.
Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.
I don’t receive glory from men.
But I know you, that you don’t have God’s love in yourselves.
I have come in my Father’s name, and you don’t receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.
How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?
“Don’t think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope.
For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me.
But if you don’t believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

stationsIntro: Jesus answered the men who wanted Him dead with wonder, judgment, voice, lamp, and accusation. Pray over each verse before you answer, and let every word drive you back to the Son who gives life.
lifeIntro: The Father has given the Son life in Himself and all judgment besides, and the Son has spoken His word to you. These practices will not keep you out of court; Christ has already done that. They are how a man walks who has passed out of death into life.
lifePulls: The Son holds all judgment and gives life to whom He desires. If you have heard His word and believed, you are not waiting on a verdict. You are living on the far side of one.
prayer: Father, You love the Son and have shown Him all that You do. Thank You that You gave Him life in Himself, and that He gave that life to me. I was dead, and His voice reached me. I heard, and I live. Close the courtroom in my head with the word of Jesus: no judgment, passed into life. Forgive me for honoring You in general and keeping Your Son at the edge. Forgive me for working for the nod of men when You have already given me Your approval in Christ. Open the Scriptures to me, so that I find Him on every page. Keep me until the hour when every grave hears His voice, and let me know that voice when it calls. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: Jesus answered the men who wanted Him dead by claiming everything: He does what the Father does, gives life to whom He desires, and holds all judgment. Then He called His witnesses — John, His works, the Father, and the Scriptures. The man who hears His word and believes is not on trial. He has eternal life now, and he has passed out of death into life. Come to Him.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the Son who gives life to whom He desires. He does not ask what you bring to the bench. He does not wait for you to climb out of the grave on your own strength. He does not hand you a ladder of Scripture and tell you to start up it. He speaks, and the dead will hear the Son of God’s voice; and those who hear will live. That voice has already reached you, and you are standing up.

Look back over the ground you have covered. You met the Word who was with God before there was any dust to cling to, and you watched Him become flesh and live among men. John the Baptist pointed Him out as the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world. He kept the good wine until last at Cana, and He named a temple He would raise in three days. He told a ruler he must be born anew, and He told the world that God so loved it He gave His one and only Son. He offered living water to a woman at Jacob’s well, sent a nobleman home to a living son, and told a man thirty-eight years on a mat to get up and walk. Part Two will set the bread of life and the light of the world in front of you, and it is the same Son holding out both.

But stand here a while first, at the end of chapter 5. The men in this chapter had the Scriptures open on their knees and missed the One every page was about. They wanted the nod of other men, and Moses stood ready to accuse them. You do not have to end where they ended. Jesus said it plainly: Don’t think that I will accuse you to the Father. The One to whom the Father gave all judgment is the One who walked up to the mat.

So carry His word out of this book and into the week in front of you. You heard. You believed the Father who sent Him. Then you have eternal life today, not someday. You will not come into judgment, because the Judge took that judgment on Himself. And you have already crossed over — out of death, into life — and no grave, no accuser, and no hard winter can carry you back across that river. The Son said so, and the Son says only what He hears from the Father.
closingVerse: Most certainly I tell you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment, but has passed out of death into life.
carry: Jesus says the man who hears His word and believes has eternal life, and doesn’t come into judgment; where on Tuesday will you still be pleading your case as if He had not already said you have passed out of death into life?
